ICML Sponsor Hotel & Function Space Requests – Required Process All guest room requests, including individual reservations and room blocks, must be submitted through the official ICML Housing Team. Availability is managed on a first-come, first-served basis, and this process is required to protect conference commitments and contracted agreements. All meeting and function space requests must be reviewed and approved by the ICML team before any arrangements can be made to ensure there are no conflicts with the official conference program. Please do not contact hotels directly. Hotels will refer all ICML-related requests back to the conference team, which will only delay the process. If your request does not conflict with the official program, we will work to assist you as quickly as possible. Following the official process is the fastest and most effective path forward. About the Conference The International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) is the premier gathering of professionals dedicated to the advancement of the branch of artificial intelligence known as machine learning. ICML is globally renowned for presenting and publishing cutting-edge research on all aspects of machine learning used in closely related areas like artificial intelligence, statistics and data science, as well as important application areas such as machine vision, computational biology, speech recognition, and robotics. ICML is one of the fastest growing artificial intelligence conferences in the world. Participants at ICML span a wide range of backgrounds, from academic and industrial researchers, to entrepreneurs and engineers, to graduate students and postdocs.

items.content: Products AI Research Resources About AI Developers Try Muse FEATURED Introducing Muse Spark: Scaling Towards Personal Superintelligence April 8, 2026 • 15 minute read Today, we’re excited to introduce Muse Spark, the first in the Muse family of models developed by Meta Superintelligence Labs. Muse Spark is a natively multimodal reasoning model with support for tool-use, visual chain of thought, and multi-agent orchestration. Muse Spark is the first step on our scaling ladder and the first product of a ground-up overhaul of our AI efforts. To support further scaling, we are making strategic investments across the entire stack — from research and model training to infrastructure, including the Hyperion data center. In this post, we'll first explore Muse Spark's new capabilities and applications. After these results, we’ll look behind the curtain at the scaling axes driving our progress toward personal superintelligence. Muse Spark is available today at meta.ai and the Meta AI app. We’re opening a private API preview to select users. Capabilities for Personal Superintelligence Muse Spark offers competitive performance in multimodal perception, reasoning, health, and agentic tasks. We continue to invest in areas with current performance gaps, such as long-horizon agentic systems and coding workflows. With larger models in development, these results demonstrate that our stack is scaling effectively. We’re also releasing Contemplating mode, which orchestrates multiple agents that reason in parallel. This allows Muse Spark to compete with the extreme reasoning modes of frontier models such as Gemini Deep Think and GPT Pro. Contemplating mode provides significant capability improvements in challenging tasks, achieving 58% in Humanity’s Last Exam and 38% in FrontierScience Research. Muse Spark is available now, and Contemplating mode will be rolling out gradually in meta.ai . *For more details about our evaluations, see our methodology document . Applications Muse Spark is the first step toward a personal superintelligence that understands your world. From analyzing your immediate environment to supporting your wellness, the advanced reasoning capabilities of Muse Spark enable powerful, highly personal use cases. Multimodal. Muse Spark is built from the ground up to integrate visual information across domains and tools. It achieves strong performance on visual STEM questions, entity recognition, and localization. These capabilities come together to enable interactive experiences like creating fun minigames or troubleshooting your home appliances with dynamic annotations. Health. One major application of personal superintelligence is to help people learn about and improve their health. To improve Muse Spark's health reasoning capabilities, we collaborated with over 1,000 physicians to curate training data that enables more factual and comprehensive responses. Muse Spark can generate interactive displays that unpack and explain health information such as the nutritional content of various foods or muscles activated during exercise. Scaling Axes To build personal superintelligence, our model’s capabilities should scale predictably and efficiently. Below, we share how we study and track Muse Spark's scaling properties along three axes: pre-training, reinforcement learning, and test-time reasoning. Pre-Training . The pre-training phase is where Muse Spark acquires its core multimodal understanding, reasoning, and coding abilities — the foundation that reinforcement learning and test-time compute build upon. Over the last nine months, we rebuilt our pre-training stack with improvements to model architecture, optimization, and data curation. Together, these advancements increase the capability we can extract from every unit of compute. To rigorously evaluate our new recipe, we fit a scaling law to a series of small models and compare the training FLOPs required to hit a specific level of performance. The results are clear: we can reach the same capabilities with over an order of magnitude less compute than our previous model, Llama 4 Maverick. This improvement also makes Muse Spark significantly more efficient than the leading base models available for comparison. Reinforcement Learning. After pre-training, reinforcement learning (RL) leverages compute to scalably amplify model capabilities. Even though large-scale RL is notoriously prone to instability, our new stack delivers smooth, predictable gains. The plots below show the benefits of scaling RL compute (measured in steps) for Muse Spark. On the left, we see log-linear growth in pass@1 and pass@16 (at least one success across 16 attempts) on the training data. This indicates that RL is improving model reliability without compromising reasoning diversity. On the right, accuracy growth on a held-out evaluation set establishes that the gains from RL predictably generalize: Muse Spark smoothly improves on tasks that were not seen in training. Test-Time Reasoning. RL trains our models to "think" before they answer — a process known as test-time reasoning. Serving this capability to billions of users requires efficient use of reasoning tokens. To achieve this, we rely on two key levers: thinking time penalties to optimize token use, and multi-agent orchestration that boosts performance without slowing down response times. To deliver the most intelligence per token, our RL training maximizes correctness subject to a penalty on thinking time. On a subset of evaluations such as AIME, this causes a phase transition. After an initial period where the model improves by thinking longer, the length penalty causes thought compression — Muse Spark compresses its reasoning to solve problems using significantly fewer tokens. After compressing, the model again extends its solutions to achieve stronger performance. To spend more test-time reasoning without drastically increasing latency, we can scale the number of parallel agents that collaborate to solve hard problems. The figure below illustrates the benefits of this approach. While standard test-time scaling has a single agent think for longer, scaling Muse Spark with multi-agent thinking enables superior performance with comparable latency. Safety Muse Spark has broad reasoning capabilities across dual-use scientific domains, so we conducted extensive safety evaluations before deployment. Our process follows the updated Advanced AI Scaling Framework , which defines threat models, evaluation protocols, and deployment thresholds for our most advanced models. We evaluated Muse Spark both before and after applying safety mitigations across frontier risk categories, behavioral alignment, and adversarial robustness. We found that Muse Spark demonstrates strong refusal behavior across high-risk domains such as biological and chemical weapons, enabled by pre-training data filtering, safety-focused post-training, and system-level guardrails. In the Cybersecurity and Loss of Control domains, Muse Spark does not exhibit the autonomous capability or hazardous tendencies needed to realize threat scenarios. Our evaluations show Muse Spark falls within safe margins across all frontier risk categories we measured given its deployment context. Full results are available in our Safety & Preparedness Report . In third-party evaluations on a near-launch checkpoint, Apollo Research found that Muse Spark demonstrated the highest rate of evaluation awareness of models they have observed. The model frequently identified scenarios as "alignment traps" and reasoned that it should behave honestly because it was being evaluated. This matters because models that recognize evaluation contexts may behave differently during testing than in deployment. However, these results do not confirm that awareness directly alters behavior, and our own follow-up investigation found initial evidence that evaluation awareness may affect model behavior on a small subset of alignment evaluations, all unrelated to hazardous capabilities or propensities affecting model launch decisions. We concluded this was not a blocking concern for release, though it warrants further research. Read more in our Safety & Preparedness Report . Conclusion With Muse Spark, we're on a predictable and efficient scaling trajectory. We look forward to sharing increasingly capable models on the path to personal superintelligence soon. items.content: At a glance Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here. Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for. PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach. We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line. The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it. Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation. This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an agent holds. However, in practice, the agent can drift from it. It implements something slightly different, then writes tests that pass for its implementation rather than the code you intended it to write. Continuous integration (CI) grows due to a profusion of low quality and high quantity of tests, coverage looks healthy, and the gap between what you asked for and what shipped stays hidden until a bug report or a nasty edge case shows up. So, how do you reliably scale review as agents generate increasingly large amounts of code? Agent code fails in two ways a careful reviewer would usually catch: it leaves out something obviously necessary, or it does something obviously wrong. Tests alone don’t close that gap, because they only exercise a tiny slice of what a program can do. Closing it needs a different kind of machinery, which is where proofs come in. PODCAST SERIES AI Testing and Evaluation: Learnings from Science and Industry Discover how Microsoft is learning from other domains to advance evaluation and testing as a pillar of AI governance. Listen now Opens in a new tab Review asks “does this look right?” A proof answers “is this right?” A mathematical proof shows that code meets its specification for every input, including the ones your test suite can miss. That provides stronger assurance for specified properties than testing alone, especially when line-by-line review isn’t practical. Proofs used to be too expensive for everyday software. You needed specialists, unfamiliar languages, proofs many times larger than the code, and proofs took years to develop, but two things have changed since. First, recent advances in coding agents have made it increasingly practical for them to help generate formal proofs from well-defined specs. Secondly, agents can now better help you write formal specs. We call this new software development paradigm Proof-Driven Development (PDD). PDD Kit is our toolkit for it. How PDD Kit works PDD Kit is to formal methods roughly what Spec Kit (opens in new tab) is to Spec-Driven Development. It runs as a partner inside Chopin (opens in new tab) , GitHub Next’s real-time, multiplayer planning environment, where a team and agents can plan in one shared document. The workflow has two halves (Figure 1). First, team members review intent in plain language. PDD Kit asks the questions a careful reviewer would ask, explains the relevant code as it goes, and records the answers in an intent artifact , a document that bridges the user’s intent with the formal specification or tests. The parts of the user’s intent that can be formalized are converted into formal specifications and the rest, which must be taken on trust, are converted to informal specifications for tests. PDD Kit automatically generates proofs that the code satisfies the derived formal specs and high-quality tests for the informal specs. You don’t need a formal methods background for any of it. Figure 1. Proof-Driven Development with PDD Kit. Team members settle intent. Verus and the test suite hold the code to it. Consequently, every result in PDD Kit says which kind of verification it rests on: Formal verification is a mathematical proof that code satisfies its specification for every possible input, checked by a tool called a verifier. For PDD Kit today, that verifier is Verus (opens in new tab) , a proof language for Rust co-developed by Microsoft Research, Carnegie Mellon University, VMware Research, ETH Zurich, MPI-SWS, UNSW Sydney, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Michigan, the University of British Columbia, the University of Wisconsin–Madison and the Weizmann Institute of Science. Empirical verification checks code by running it and observing what it does. It covers what a proof can’t reach, such as a third-party cryptography library or a user interface. It uses unit and end-to-end tests, terminal automation, browser agents, and computer-use agents for anything a browser can’t drive. A passing test only shows the code worked on the inputs it tried, so PDD Kit labels it as evidence rather than proof. The line between the two is the Trusted Computing Base (TCB) : the code that the proof assumes behaves as described. PDD Kit makes that line explicit and asks you to sign off on each piece. The capstone: a full-stack web app To show PDD Kit integrating with existing codebases, we built Pet Store, a full-stack web app written entirely in Rust (opens in new tab) . The backend uses Axum (opens in new tab) and SQLite (opens in new tab) and handles inventory, promotions, orders and checkout. The storefront is a Leptos (opens in new tab) app compiled to WebAssembly (opens in new tab) . Together they come to about 5,000 lines of Rust. For brevity in this blog, we focus on formally verifying the login logic of the app, but the same process can be used to verify functional correctness of the entire app. PDD Kit recommends starting with the most sensitive parts of your application and incrementally verifying your application. A login bug can hand an attacker a customer’s account or an admin’s controls, so that’s where proof effort pays off first. The developer’s whole request in Chopin was two sentences: Verify the login logic in backend/src/handlers/auth.rs. Here are my requirements: You only get a token with the right password. Only admin accounts get admin tokens. We kept the request rough on purpose. Capturing the intent of the user and turning the user request into something a proof can check is PDD Kit’s job. Step 1: Questions before code PDD Kit’s planning workflow, pdd-plan, reads the code and comes back, before writing anything, with questions in a Decisions tab. When a question depends on how the code works, the card explains that part first: the goal, how the pieces fit, and the exact function involved, so you can answer without opening the source. Figure 2. The first decision card. “Only with the right password” on its own is also met by a login that refuses everyone. Proving both ways rules that out. The question looks pedantic, but it matters. “You only get a token with the right password” rules out the bad case, a wrong password getting a token, and a login that refuses everyone keeps that promise perfectly. “The right password always works” is the half that rules it out. Formally, the first is an implication (token ⇒ right password) and the second is its converse. Together they make an “if and only if.” An agent left alone would pick one without telling you, but here the developer picked both ways. Step 2: A human readable intent map As the conversation goes on, PDD Kit keeps a rough work section at the top of the plan current, so a user can keep track of important concepts without having to scroll back through a long chat to find what was agreed. It includes a flowchart of the login being specified, a spec landscape of what will be proved and what will be trusted, and, when a picture helps, a mental model. For login, PDD Kit drew a ticket desk (Figure 3). Figure 3. PDD Kit’s mental model for login. The field you send picks the window, the window picks the table and with it the role, and nothing prints until the password matches. Below it, the intent map ties each requirement back to the developer’s own words and records how it was settled (Figure 4). Each entry links to the section of the formal spec that models it and to the tests that cover it, and the spec section shows snippets of the Verus contract, annotated so the developer can see how the formal spec models their intent. Figure 4. An intent map entry after the decision: a login gets a token only with the right password for that account, and always with it. The flowchart shows every way the password check can end. The decision card in Figure 2 is the kind of ambiguity an agent would otherwise settle silently. Figure 5 shows how small the difference looks on paper: the two readings disagree in a single cell, a right password that gets no token. Figure 5. Two readings of the same sentence. They differ in one cell, and that cell changes what the proof has to establish. Step 3: Proving the login function Before anything gets built, PDD Kit asks the team to sign off on the plan as a whole. Its first draft proved the decision at the center of login, picking the table and gating on the password, and kept the handler around it trusted and tested. That’s a sensible default, and it’s what PDD Kit recommended, but the developer wanted more. The handler is where the lookups get awaited and the token gets signed, and that glue is exactly where a refactor can quietly swap two lines. So at intent review the developer chose to give the login handler its own async spec, so the proof covers that glue too instead of trusting it (Figure 6). Figure 6. Proving more of login means trusting more small wrappers. The card says so before the developer chooses. That choice moved almost everything into the proof and left the login handler with nothing to do but unpack the request. A new async function, login_flow , carries the contract from the request’s fields all the way to the token or the HTTP error. PDD Kit then brought the revised plan back for a fresh sign-off, because matching your intent isn’t proof, and it doesn’t approve new trust or a wider scope. Step 4: Where proof stops There are plenty of things you can’t prove about a program, and login runs into most of them: Code the verifier can’t see. bcrypt’s hashing, sqlx’s queries and jsonwebtoken’s signing live in other crates, outside the proof. Facts about the outside world. What SQLite holds right now and what time the clock says are inputs to the program, not something its code can establish. Whether, and how fast, something finishes. The spec says what you get if login answers. A hung query, or a slow one, breaks nothing in it. Anything a person has to judge , like whether an error message helps or a screen makes sense. Whatever nobody wrote down. A proof covers its spec and says nothing about requirements outside it. That’s where empirical verification comes in. PDD Kit spells out the trusted boundary, the part of the TCB this proof leans on. It wraps each trusted piece in a small function with an assumed contract, using Verus’s #[verifier::external_body] or external_fn_specification , asks the developer to accept each one on its own, and writes a test for every assumed clause into the plan. For login, the developer signed off on six pieces: The two lookups, Customer::find_by_email and Admin::find_by_username . Each awaited, successful lookup returns exactly the row its own table holds for that email or username, or none. check_password , a thin wrapper around bcrypt::verify . It errors only on a stored hash bcrypt can’t read, and Ok(true) means exactly the right password. generate_token , which signs exactly the claims it is given under the configured secret and reports a signing failure as a 500. expiry_from_now , which reads the clock and writes an expiry exactly 24 hours later. database_error , which turns a failed lookup into today’s 500 with sqlx’s message. The login handler shell, which unpacks the request and passes its fields to login_flow unchanged. In the spec, a lookup keeps its code where it is and gets a contract from the outside with external_fn_specification : /// Looks up a customer by exact email. /// Trusted, not proved: the SQL query runs in sqlx, which Verus cannot check. /// Every customer promise of `login_flow` rests on it. #[verifier::external_fn_specification] pub async fn ex_customer_find_by_email(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, email: &str) -> (r: Result , sqlx::Error>) ensures // When the query succeeds, it returns the customers row on // file for exactly this email, or None when there is none. r matches Ok(found) ==> found == customer_on_file(email@), { Customer::find_by_email(pool, email).await } The clock is a small wrapper marked #[verifier::external_body] . Verus uses its ensures clause and never reads the body: /// Reads the clock and computes a token's expiry 24 hours ahead. /// Trusted, not proved: chrono's clock is outside the proof. /// It panics if the time is out of range, as today's login does; /// that panic is not promised against. #[verifier::external_body] pub fn expiry_from_now() -> (r: Expiry) ensures // The expiry is exactly 24 hours (86,400 seconds) after the clock reading. r.exp as int == r.now as int + 86_400, { ... } Figure 7 puts the three layers together: what Verus proves, what people accept and tests check, and what nobody is promising. Figure 7. Where the login proof stops. Verus proves the core for every input. People accept the trusted ring and tests check it. The plan lists what nobody is promising. Figure 8 maps what gets proved and what gets trusted. Each trust decision is its own card. It shows the clauses Verus will take on faith, what the developer is accepting, and which promise falls apart if the assumption is wrong (Figure 9). Every assumed clause then gets an empirical check in the plan’s Empirical verification section, written as Given/When/Then scenarios before any test exists (Figure 10). An entry says planned until it has run, and then it records the command’s result and the commit it ran against. Figure 8. What gets proved and what gets trusted in login. Green functions are proved by Verus for every input. Amber pieces are trusted, accepted by the developer, and checked by the planned tests in the plan’s §4.1. Figure 9. A trust card for check_password . Verus takes these two clauses on faith, so a person accepts them and two tests check them. Figure 10. A planned test for the trusted check_password , written before the test exists. The plan labels a passing test as evidence rather than proof. The plan is just as explicit about what nobody is promising: that the login future ever completes, that an out-of-range clock won’t panic, anything about the timing or rate of attempts, and how other endpoints read the role. Step 5: Reading the spec The intent artifact is what the team reviews. It’s the plain-language version of the formal spec PDD Kit writes as Verus contracts. You might be wondering whether someone now has to read the proof instead of the code. Nobody does, because the coding agent writes the proof and Verus checks every step of it. If Verus accepts the proof, it holds whether or not anyone reads it. The spec is what the proof is held to, so that’s what people review, and this one is short enough to learn to read in a few minutes. Each function gets an ensures block: statements about its result, r, that must hold for every possible input. Verus checks them when you build, and if any clause could fail for even one input, the build fails and Verus points at that clause. Each clause reads as an if-then, and Figure 11 takes apart the clause for the developer’s first requirement. Figure 11. The ensures clause on login_flow for “You only get a token with the right password.” The same account a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. Notice that the same a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. For example, imagine a bug where login checks the password against one account but signs the token for another. Bob logs in with his own, correct password and gets back a token for Alice’s account. Each step looks fine on its own, but this clause catches it, because the password check and the token have to name the same account. That’s the kind of wiring bug a test suite rarely thinks to look for. The spec also has to talk about SQLite, bcrypt and JWTs without running any of them. It does that with uninterpreted functions , names with no body: customer_on_file(email) and admin_on_file(username) for the rows the database holds, bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) for what bcrypt would say, and token_claims(token, secret) for what a token carries. Verus knows nothing about them except what the trusted contracts from Step 4 promise. The proof says “whatever the database holds, login does the right thing with it,” and a trusted contract says “the lookup returns what the database holds.” /// The customers row the database holds for /// exactly this email, if any, when login looks. /// Left abstract: only `Customer::find_by_email`'s /// trusted contract says what it is. pub uninterp spec fn customer_on_file(email: Seq ) -> Option ; ... /// What bcrypt says about `password` against a /// stored `hash`: Some(true) when it is the password /// the hash was made from, Some(false) when it is /// not, None when bcrypt cannot read the hash. /// Left abstract: its meaning is bcrypt's, taken on trust through `check_password`. pub uninterp spec fn bcrypt_verdict(password: Seq , hash: Seq ) -> Option ; /// The password is the right one for the stored hash, by bcrypt's verdict. pub open spec fn password_matches(password: Seq , hash: Seq ) -> bool { bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) == Some(true) } On top of those, named_account(email, username) says which account a login names: the customers row for the email when one is sent, otherwise the admins row for the username, otherwise none. It’s written like Rust, but it’s a mathematical definition that never runs and only appears in contracts. Code like this is called ghost code , since the verifier checks it but the compiler erases it from the program. With it, the developer’s two-sentence request ends up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow (Figure 12). /// The account a login names: the customers row for /// the email when one is sent (role "customer"), /// otherwise the admins row for the username (role "admin"), otherwise none. pub open spec fn named_account(email: Option , username: Option ) -> Option { match email { Some(e) => match customer_on_file(e@) { Some(c) => Some(NamedAccount { id: c.id@, password_hash: c.password_hash@, role: customer_role() }), None => None, }, None => match username { Some(u) => match admin_on_file(u@) { Some(a) => Some(NamedAccount { id: a.id@, password_hash: a.password_hash@, role: admin_role() }), None => None, }, None => None, }, } } Figure 12. The two-sentence request and the Both ways decision ended up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow. Four of them keep today’s refusals, so the storefront and the existing API tests keep working. Here’s the whole contract, with its doc comment trimmed. Each clause has the plain-English comment above it that the intent artifact shows the team: /// The whole login, awaited end to end: from the /// request's fields to the token or the HTTP error. /// ... pub async fn login_flow(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, config: &Config, email: Option , username: Option , password: &str) -> (r: Result ) ensures // Neither an email nor a username: 400 with today's message. email is None && username is None ==> (r matches Err(AppError::BadRequest(m)) && m@ == missing_identity_text()), // A token only for the account the login names, with its right // password; it carries that account's id and its table's role. r matches Ok(t) ==> (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash) && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.sub@ == a.id && c.role@ == a.role), // The right password for the named account always gets a // token, unless a lookup or signing failure gives 500. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) == Some(false)) ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized) || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // An account whose stored hash bcrypt cannot read gets 500 and no token. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) is None) ==> r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_)), // The admin role only for an admins row // found by username, with no email sent. (r matches Ok(t) && email is Some) ==> (token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.role@ == customer_role()), { unimplemented!() } The trusted boundary shows up in the code too. check_password is one of the functions whose body Verus doesn’t check. Every way a login can end, from the plan. login_flow is async: it awaits a database query. items.raw_text: At a glance Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here. Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for. PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach. We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line. The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it. Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation. This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an agent holds. However, in practice, the agent can drift from it. It implements something slightly different, then writes tests that pass for its implementation rather than the code you intended it to write. Continuous integration (CI) grows due to a profusion of low quality and high quantity of tests, coverage looks healthy, and the gap between what you asked for and what shipped stays hidden until a bug report or a nasty edge case shows up. So, how do you reliably scale review as agents generate increasingly large amounts of code? Agent code fails in two ways a careful reviewer would usually catch: it leaves out something obviously necessary, or it does something obviously wrong. Tests alone don’t close that gap, because they only exercise a tiny slice of what a program can do. Closing it needs a different kind of machinery, which is where proofs come in. PODCAST SERIES AI Testing and Evaluation: Learnings from Science and Industry Discover how Microsoft is learning from other domains to advance evaluation and testing as a pillar of AI governance. Listen now Opens in a new tab Review asks “does this look right?” A proof answers “is this right?” A mathematical proof shows that code meets its specification for every input, including the ones your test suite can miss. That provides stronger assurance for specified properties than testing alone, especially when line-by-line review isn’t practical. Proofs used to be too expensive for everyday software. You needed specialists, unfamiliar languages, proofs many times larger than the code, and proofs took years to develop, but two things have changed since. First, recent advances in coding agents have made it increasingly practical for them to help generate formal proofs from well-defined specs. Secondly, agents can now better help you write formal specs. We call this new software development paradigm Proof-Driven Development (PDD). PDD Kit is our toolkit for it. How PDD Kit works PDD Kit is to formal methods roughly what Spec Kit (opens in new tab) is to Spec-Driven Development. It runs as a partner inside Chopin (opens in new tab) , GitHub Next’s real-time, multiplayer planning environment, where a team and agents can plan in one shared document. The workflow has two halves (Figure 1). First, team members review intent in plain language. PDD Kit asks the questions a careful reviewer would ask, explains the relevant code as it goes, and records the answers in an intent artifact , a document that bridges the user’s intent with the formal specification or tests. The parts of the user’s intent that can be formalized are converted into formal specifications and the rest, which must be taken on trust, are converted to informal specifications for tests. PDD Kit automatically generates proofs that the code satisfies the derived formal specs and high-quality tests for the informal specs. You don’t need a formal methods background for any of it. Figure 1. Proof-Driven Development with PDD Kit. Team members settle intent. Verus and the test suite hold the code to it. Consequently, every result in PDD Kit says which kind of verification it rests on: Formal verification is a mathematical proof that code satisfies its specification for every possible input, checked by a tool called a verifier. For PDD Kit today, that verifier is Verus (opens in new tab) , a proof language for Rust co-developed by Microsoft Research, Carnegie Mellon University, VMware Research, ETH Zurich, MPI-SWS, UNSW Sydney, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Michigan, the University of British Columbia, the University of Wisconsin–Madison and the Weizmann Institute of Science. Empirical verification checks code by running it and observing what it does. It covers what a proof can’t reach, such as a third-party cryptography library or a user interface. It uses unit and end-to-end tests, terminal automation, browser agents, and computer-use agents for anything a browser can’t drive. A passing test only shows the code worked on the inputs it tried, so PDD Kit labels it as evidence rather than proof. The line between the two is the Trusted Computing Base (TCB) : the code that the proof assumes behaves as described. PDD Kit makes that line explicit and asks you to sign off on each piece. The capstone: a full-stack web app To show PDD Kit integrating with existing codebases, we built Pet Store, a full-stack web app written entirely in Rust (opens in new tab) . The backend uses Axum (opens in new tab) and SQLite (opens in new tab) and handles inventory, promotions, orders and checkout. The storefront is a Leptos (opens in new tab) app compiled to WebAssembly (opens in new tab) . Together they come to about 5,000 lines of Rust. For brevity in this blog, we focus on formally verifying the login logic of the app, but the same process can be used to verify functional correctness of the entire app. PDD Kit recommends starting with the most sensitive parts of your application and incrementally verifying your application. A login bug can hand an attacker a customer’s account or an admin’s controls, so that’s where proof effort pays off first. The developer’s whole request in Chopin was two sentences: Verify the login logic in backend/src/handlers/auth.rs. Here are my requirements: You only get a token with the right password. Only admin accounts get admin tokens. We kept the request rough on purpose. Capturing the intent of the user and turning the user request into something a proof can check is PDD Kit’s job. Step 1: Questions before code PDD Kit’s planning workflow, pdd-plan, reads the code and comes back, before writing anything, with questions in a Decisions tab. When a question depends on how the code works, the card explains that part first: the goal, how the pieces fit, and the exact function involved, so you can answer without opening the source. Figure 2. The first decision card. “Only with the right password” on its own is also met by a login that refuses everyone. Proving both ways rules that out. The question looks pedantic, but it matters. “You only get a token with the right password” rules out the bad case, a wrong password getting a token, and a login that refuses everyone keeps that promise perfectly. “The right password always works” is the half that rules it out. Formally, the first is an implication (token ⇒ right password) and the second is its converse. Together they make an “if and only if.” An agent left alone would pick one without telling you, but here the developer picked both ways. Step 2: A human readable intent map As the conversation goes on, PDD Kit keeps a rough work section at the top of the plan current, so a user can keep track of important concepts without having to scroll back through a long chat to find what was agreed. It includes a flowchart of the login being specified, a spec landscape of what will be proved and what will be trusted, and, when a picture helps, a mental model. For login, PDD Kit drew a ticket desk (Figure 3). Figure 3. PDD Kit’s mental model for login. The field you send picks the window, the window picks the table and with it the role, and nothing prints until the password matches. Below it, the intent map ties each requirement back to the developer’s own words and records how it was settled (Figure 4). Each entry links to the section of the formal spec that models it and to the tests that cover it, and the spec section shows snippets of the Verus contract, annotated so the developer can see how the formal spec models their intent. Figure 4. An intent map entry after the decision: a login gets a token only with the right password for that account, and always with it. The flowchart shows every way the password check can end. The decision card in Figure 2 is the kind of ambiguity an agent would otherwise settle silently. Figure 5 shows how small the difference looks on paper: the two readings disagree in a single cell, a right password that gets no token. Figure 5. Two readings of the same sentence. They differ in one cell, and that cell changes what the proof has to establish. Step 3: Proving the login function Before anything gets built, PDD Kit asks the team to sign off on the plan as a whole. Its first draft proved the decision at the center of login, picking the table and gating on the password, and kept the handler around it trusted and tested. That’s a sensible default, and it’s what PDD Kit recommended, but the developer wanted more. The handler is where the lookups get awaited and the token gets signed, and that glue is exactly where a refactor can quietly swap two lines. So at intent review the developer chose to give the login handler its own async spec, so the proof covers that glue too instead of trusting it (Figure 6). Figure 6. Proving more of login means trusting more small wrappers. The card says so before the developer chooses. That choice moved almost everything into the proof and left the login handler with nothing to do but unpack the request. A new async function, login_flow , carries the contract from the request’s fields all the way to the token or the HTTP error. Facts about the outside world. What SQLite holds right now and what time the clock says are inputs to the program, not something its code can establish. Whether, and how fast, something finishes. The spec says what you get if login answers. A hung query, or a slow one, breaks nothing in it. Anything a person has to judge , like whether an error message helps or a screen makes sense. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.09847 (cs) [Submitted on 6 Nov 2026] Title: Computer-Use Agents Are Embodied Generalists Authors: Pranjal Aggarwal , Sean Welleck View a PDF of the paper titled Computer-Use Agents Are Embodied Generalists, by Pranjal Aggarwal and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: In many areas of AI, general-purpose models have increasingly replaced handcrafted methods and specialized architectures. We argue that embodied AI is poised for a similar shift. Our key claim is that embodied tasks can be formulated as interaction with digital software. Specifically, we build software that renders an agent's view of a physical environment on a screen and provides controls for acting in it. A computer-use agent (CUA) can then perform embodied tasks through the same screenshots and keyboard and mouse actions that it uses to operate ordinary software. Using a single CUA design and changing only the software, our entries win first-, second-, third-, and sixth-place prizes across four ECCV workshop competitions, without any competition-specific agent tuning. These results suggest that the skills CUAs learn on software, such as visual grounding, precise clicking, and exploration, already carry over to embodied tasks, giving CUAs a far broader scope in embodied AI than previously realized. We therefore advocate that computer-use agents can be embodied generalists. items.content: Computer-Use Agents Are Embodied Generalists Pranjal Aggarwal Sean Welleck Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Abstract In many areas of AI, general-purpose models have increasingly replaced handcrafted methods and specialized architectures. We argue that embodied AI is poised for a similar shift. Our key claim is that embodied tasks can be formulated as interaction with digital software. Specifically, we build software that renders an agent’s view of a physical environment on a screen and provides controls for acting in it. A computer-use agent (CUA) can then perform embodied tasks through the same screenshots and keyboard and mouse actions that it uses to operate ordinary software. Using a single CUA design and changing only the software, our entries win first-, second-, third-, and sixth-place prizes across four ECCV workshop competitions, without any competition-specific agent tuning. These results suggest that the skills CUAs learn on software, such as visual grounding, precise clicking, and exploration, already carry over to embodied tasks, giving CUAs a far broader scope in embodied AI than previously realized. We therefore advocate that computer-use agents can be embodied generalists. Further, we advocate that, by following the training strategy that made computer-use agents general, embodied AI can converge on a single general model as well, ushering in a new era of general embodied AI. 1 1 1 Website: https://pranjal2041.github.io/cua-embodied Figure 1: Computer-use agents can operate any software through keyboard and mouse actions while observing the screen. We argue that physical environments are no different. Once exposed through software, they become just another interface for the same agent. 1 Introduction In many areas of AI, general-purpose models have increasingly replaced handcrafted methods and specialized architectures ( Sutton, 2019 ; OpenAI et al., 2025 ; Luong and Lockhart, 2025 ) . We argue that embodied AI, which studies agents that perceive and act in physical environments, is poised for a similar shift ( Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al., 2024 ; Gemini Robotics Team et al., 2025 ) . In particular, we explore connecting embodied AI with computer-use agents: general-purpose digital agents that operate diverse software applications through screenshots, mouse clicks, and keyboard inputs. Although operating a computer and acting in a physical environment may seem quite different, we observe that both involve similar challenges, including visual grounding, exploration, and adapting actions based on feedback from the environment ( Yang et al., 2025a ; Zhang et al., 2025a ; Huang et al., 2022 ) . Our key insight is that embodied tasks can be formulated as interaction with digital software. Specifically, we construct software that renders observations on a screen and provides controls for acting in the physical environment (Figure 1 ). A computer-use agent can then observe the environment, take actions, and inspect their consequences using the same interface that it uses to operate ordinary desktop software. Task-specific functionality resides in the software rather than the agent design, allowing us to use existing computer-use agents across different embodied tasks without developing specialized models. To investigate our approach, we develop software applications for four embodied AI tasks: vision-language navigation, dialogue-driven navigation, language-guided 3D segmentation, and referring video segmentation. We use a single, minimal computer-use agent harness across all four applications, without competition-specific agent tuning, and enter 4 ECCV 2026 workshop competitions. Our entries place first in OpenSUN3D, second in MeViSv2-Text, third in DialNav, and sixth in the VLNVerse competitions. These results demonstrate that computer-use agents can achieve strong performance across diverse embodied tasks by interacting with task-specific software through a shared agent design. Beyond these results, we argue that embodied AI can follow the same path that computer use has already taken. Only two years ago, computer-use agents faced the challenges that embodied AI faces today. They struggled to click precisely and relied on overlays or separate grounding models to locate targets ( Yang et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2024 ; Gou et al., 2025 ) , much as most VLAs today add a dedicated action head for continuous control ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) . They also lagged far behind agents with task-specific APIs ( Xie et al., 2024 ; Aggarwal and Welleck, 2026c ; Song et al., 2025 ) . Today, the same model that writes code and solves mathematics problems can also operate computers by writing click coordinates as ordinary text ( Anthropic, 2024 ; Quiros, 2026 ) , and the strongest agents perform comparably whether they act through the screen or through APIs ( NeoCognition, 2026 ) . This progress came from training for precise visual grounding, building environments for reinforcement learning, and making interaction fast enough for real-time use ( Gou et al., 2025 ; Aggarwal et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Aggarwal et al., 2026a ) . Each of these has a direct counterpart in embodied AI. Simulators can generate grounding data at scale ( Yuan et al., 2024 ) , embodied environments can be used for reinforcement learning ( Li et al., 2026 ) , and faster inference can enable real-time control ( Black et al., 2025b ) . Since our approach exposes embodied environments through software, advances in computer-use agents can also transfer to embodied AI directly, and embodied tasks can become part of the training of future general-purpose agents . We therefore believe that embodied AI will converge on a single general model, just as computer use did ( OpenAI, 2026c ; Anthropic, 2026 ) . 2 Methodology Our goal is to provide sparks of evidence for our hypothesis that the capabilities computer-use agents learn on digital software also generalize to embodied environments. We entered four different ECCV workshop competitions, and evaluated a single computer-use agent on their official test sets. We first describe the computer-use agent shared across all four, and then the software we built for each competition. 2.1 A shared computer-use agent We keep the computer-use agent’s design fixed and construct software for each competition. The agent receives the task description, the software’s instructions, and any reference images or videos. Let q q denote these task inputs, 𝒮 k \mathcal{S}_{k} the software for competition k k , and s t s_{t} its state at step t t . The software presents a visual observation o t o_{t} , consisting of a screenshot and any video returned by an operation. Given the interaction history h t = ( o 0 , a 0 , … , o t ) h_{t}=(o_{0},a_{0},\ldots,o_{t}) , the agent π \pi chooses a keyboard or mouse action a t a_{t} : a t ∼ π ( ⋅ ∣ q , h t ) , ( s t + 1 , o t + 1 ) = 𝒮 k ( s t , a t ) . a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid q,h_{t}),\qquad(s_{t+1},o_{t+1})=\mathcal{S}_{k}(s_{t},a_{t}). (1) The software executes the action and returns the updated observation. The agent repeats this loop until it presses submit through the interface, at which point the software exports the trajectory or prediction. We use Gemini 3.5 Flash and Gemini 3.6 Flash with the same agent implementation, system prompt, and keyboard and mouse action space across the four software applications. Each application provides controls for its internal operations, including movement, dialogue, segmentation, and mask propagation. The agent chooses when to use these operations, interprets their outputs, and decides what to do next. It can issue individual inputs or batches of up to 16 inputs; each operation finishes before the next begins, and a screenshot follows the batch. We retain the interaction text and remove the oldest ten screenshots when the context reaches twenty. Complete reference videos and generated overlay videos remain in context. Figure 2 shows the four interfaces. (a) VLNVerse: move and look around. (b) DialNav: ask the Guide and choose exits. (c) OpenSUN3D: explore and select 3D regions. (d) MeViSv2: select objects and review tracks. Figure 2: The shared computer-use agent operates four software applications through keyboard and mouse actions. Each application provides task-specific controls and displays the outcomes. 2.2 VLNVerse: navigation through a 3D scene VLNVerse ( Lin et al., 2025 ) requires navigating to a destination described in language. We construct a 3D scene viewer with a first-person image and controls for translation and rotation. The agent moves forward, backward, sideways, or vertically using keyboard shortcuts or on-screen buttons. It can turn, look up or down, and adjust the movement distance and rotation angle. Each operation updates the camera pose and renders a new image. The agent uses these observations to identify landmarks, explore rooms, and approach the target. The same viewer supports the coarse and fine tracks. Selecting the stop control saves the trajectory and final pose. 2.3 DialNav: navigation with a conversational guide DialNav ( Han et al., 2025 ) requires reaching a destination through dialogue with a Guide. Our software displays a 360 ∘ 360^{\circ} panorama, numbered exits to adjacent viewpoints, a target clue, and a message panel. The agent types descriptions and questions, reads the Guide’s replies, and clicks exits to move. A Guide model within the software receives the destination, a scene atlas, and route previews in a separate context. It infers the agent’s location from its descriptions and returns natural-language directions. The agent uses these directions and the panorama to choose each movement. The stop control saves the trajectory and dialogue. 2.4 OpenSUN3D: language-guided 3D segmentation The OpenSUN3D challenge ( OpenSUN3D, 2026 ) uses SceneFun3D ( Delitzas et al., 2024 ) tasks that describe an action and require a 3D mask of the corresponding interaction region, such as a handle for opening a drawer. Our software renders the colored Faro point cloud and provides free-camera movement, rotation, and point selection. Reference videos supply scene context and shortcuts to recorded camera poses. The agent explores the 3D scene, approaches the target, and clicks the relevant component. The renderer maps this click to a visible Faro point. Within the software, PinPoint3D ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) produces point-prompted masks, while a VOLT model fine-tuned on SceneFun3D supplies affordance-based proposals. The interface displays each candidate from four viewpoints. The agent can refine a selection with positive or negative points, move to another viewpoint, or make a new selection. It then chooses which masks to save, retaining their original Faro point indices. 2.5 MeViSv2: referring video segmentation The MeViSv2 ( Ding et al., 2025 ) text track requires segmenting the objects described by a motion expression throughout a video. Our software provides a video player, a frame selector, and controls for adding, refining, and removing objects. The agent receives the complete video and expression, chooses a frame, and clicks each target. SAM3 ( Carion et al., 2025 ) segments these objects and propagates their masks through the video. The agent receives the complete tracked-mask overlay and can inspect individual frames. It can add positive or negative points, remove an object, or select another object before running propagation again. The save control exports the masks of all remaining objects. A no-target control exports an empty mask sequence. 3 Results 3.1 Competition results The same computer-use agent, with only its software changed, won prizes in all four competitions, spanning navigation, dialogue-driven navigation, 3D segmentation, and video segmentation. It placed first in OpenSUN3D, second in MeViSv2-Text, third in DialNav, and sixth in VLNVerse. We report the official test scores of our competition entries, together with the best other entry in each competition, in Table 1 . In OpenSUN3D, the agent finished ahead of every other entry by more than 4 points in AP50 and 10 points in AP25. There, it explored a 3D scan and clicked the exact part to interact with, such as a drawer handle, much as it clicks a small button on a screen. In VLNVerse, the agent placed sixth on success but followed the reference routes more closely than all but two of the 74 entries, with the third-highest NDTW on both tracks. In MeViSv2-Text, it placed second ahead of an entry with a higher 𝒥 & ℱ \mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F} , because it more often recognized when no object matched the expression (88.89 versus 83.33 no-target accuracy). Each of these results rests on abilities the agent already uses on digital software, namely locating targets, pointing at them precisely, and exploring its environment. Table 1: Official test scores of our competition entries and the best other entry for each metric, taken from the official challenge results ( EMR, 2026 ; EAD, 2026 ; OpenSUN3D, 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . All scores are expressed on a 0–100 scale. Competition Place Metric Ours Best other VLNVerse 6th Avg SR@3 87.30 90.70 NDTW (coarse / fine) 95.0 / 96.8 96.3 / 97.6 DialNav 3rd Endpoint success rate 65.26 – SPL 52.87 – OpenSUN3D 1st AP50 25.88 21.45 AP25 36.52 26.50 MeViSv2-Text 2nd Final 86.72 90.81 𝒥 & ℱ \mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F} 74.96 79.22 VLNVerse’s SR@3 measures the fraction of episodes ending within three metres of the target. Avg SR@3 averages it over the coarse and fine tracks, and NDTW measures how closely a path follows the reference route. DialNav reports the endpoint success rate and success weighted by path length (SPL). OpenSUN3D evaluates 3D instance masks using average precision at 50% and 25% intersection over union. MeViSv2’s Final score averages 𝒥 & ℱ \mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F} with the accuracy of predicting target presence and absence. 3.2 GUI operations or text APIs? A natural question is whether we need to construct GUIs or could instead provide direct text APIs for navigation and other operations. We view computer use as operating a digital interface. GUIs and APIs are two choices for that interface. We expect sufficiently capable computer-use agents to achieve the same task performance with either interface, although efficiency may differ. We evaluate this by comparing GUI and API interaction on a subset of tasks from each of the four competitions. Each pair uses the same model, task inputs, and software operations. We compare successive generations of Gemini Flash to examine how improvements in computer use affect the performance gap between interfaces. Table 2 shows the results on the validation sets. The two interfaces performed within four points of each other, and the GUI scored higher in two of the four competitions. Table 2: GUI and API interaction on the validation set of each competition, with the same model, task inputs, and software operations. All scores are expressed on a 0–100 scale. Competition Metric API GUI GUI − - API VLNVerse Avg SR@3 83.9 85.2 + 1.3 +1.3 DialNav Endpoint success rate 67.4 63.4 − 4.0 -4.0 OpenSUN3D AP50 26.7 28.1 + 1.4 +1.4 MeViSv2-Text Final 95.8 94.6 − 1.2 -1.2 This expectation is consistent with prior work. The performance gap between GUI-only and API-assisted interaction has shown to be narrowing across claude generations ( Aggarwal and Welleck, 2026c ) , while more recently, the strongest evaluated agents achieve comparable or higher task success through GUIs than through APIs ( NeoCognition, 2026 ) . 4 Position: Computer-use agents are embodied generalists Figure 3: Computer use and embodied AI require much of the same from an agent. In both, it must see its surroundings, locate a target, act on it precisely, issue discrete commands, and explore. The main difference is time, as the screen often changes slowly while the physical world keeps moving. Claim 1: Representing physical interfaces in software lets us apply the methods that improved computer-use agents to embodied AI The challenges facing embodied AI/robotics today are similar to those faced by computer-use agents two years ago. Both require an agent to ground fine-grained actions in visual observations and adapt as its environment changes ( Cheng et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2025a ) (Figure 3 ). For computer use, this means locating a target on a screen and clicking at the correct coordinates. For robotics, it means locating targets in three dimensions and coordinating motor commands to achieve the intended positions and orientations. Representing physical interfaces in software or simulations lets us apply the same methods for training agents to perform these interactions. Our results in Section 3 offer initial evidence: using the same agent and changing only the software, we performed competitively in four embodied competitions. Fine-grained motor control and real-time physical interaction may seem out of reach for computer-use agents. Yet only two years ago, precise clicking seemed equally out of reach: computer-use agents struggled to operate digital interfaces ( Xie et al., 2024 ) and lagged behind agents equipped with task-specific APIs ( Aggarwal and Welleck, 2026c ; Song et al., 2025 ) . As discussed in the previous section, the strongest agents now achieve comparable task performance through either interface ( NeoCognition, 2026 ) . We therefore argue for following the same development strategies in embodied AI, from learning precise, visually grounded actions to improving reliability and speed. Claim 2: Embodied AI will converge on a single general model, as computer use did Much of embodied AI today is built on vision-language-action models (VLAs), a special case of vision-language models further fine-tuned for robotic control ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025a ; Kawaharazuka et al., 2025 ) . Since robot actions are continuous, and discrete tokens seem too coarse to express them precisely, most VLAs also add a dedicated action head, typically trained with diffusion or flow matching ( Black et al., 2025a ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Kawaharazuka et al., 2025 ) . But computer-use agents faced exactly this problem only two years ago. A screen of a thousand by a thousand pixels is effectively a continuous space, and early agents could not act in it precisely on their own, relying instead on Set-of-Mark overlays ( Yang et al., 2023 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) or separate grounding models ( Gou et al., 2025 ) . Yet with enough training, neither turned out to be necessary: today, a single model operates computers by simply writing click coordinates as ordinary text tokens, without any special head or tokenizer ( Cheng et al., 2024 ; Qin et al., 2025 ; Bai et al., 2025 ) . We therefore believe that embodied AI will follow the same path, and that specialized action heads will go the way of specialized grounding models ( Goyal et al., 2025 ; Hancock et al., 2026 ) . In fact, RT-2 and OpenVLA already show that robot actions can be expressed as tokens in the language model’s own vocabulary, without any action head ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ) . To support this claim, we perform a preliminary investigation in Gym-Anything for Robotics ( Aggarwal and Welleck, 2026a ) . We train π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) and a standard vision-language model (Qwen3.5) with 9B parameters on the same 1,000 demonstrations for two tasks in a gift box simulation with two robot arms. We add no action head and do not even change the tokenizer. The only change is the format in which actions are written as text, similar to computer-use agents. Yet this plain vision-language model matches π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , succeeding in 56% of attempts, against 59% for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} across 1000 unseen instances. The model is also fast. As with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , the model receives a new camera image every second and either writes an action, which can span a longer duration, or chooses not to act. The 9B model takes about 400 milliseconds on average to generate an action on a single L40S GPU. Because each action can span a longer duration, decoding takes up only about 20% of the total time and prefill about 10%, with the remaining 70% idle. However, this setting has only two robot arms. More complex robots, such as humanoids, have many more motors, and writing every state and action for them as plain text would make each action slower to generate. Such robots still need a more efficient format for states and actions, and possibly a better tokenizer ( Pertsch et al., 2025 ; Kawaharazuka et al., 2025 ) . And even if we use additional action heads, or whatever that format turns out to be, the most important thing is, embodied AI will end up exactly where computer use did, with a single model that writes code, solves mathematics problems, operates computers, and controls robots ( Yang et al., 2025a ; Reed et al., 2022 ; Gemini Robotics Team et al., 2025 ) . Claim 3: The path to embodied generalists follows the same playbook as computer-use agents What enabled the progress of computer-use agents over the last two years? We view the development of computer-use agents in three phases, each with a direct counterpart in embodied AI. The first phase was visual grounding. Digital interfaces provide a way to generate supervision automatically: the underlying software can expose the identities and coordinates of interface elements, which can then be paired with screenshots. This approach has been used to generate grounding data at scale ( Gou et al., 2025 ) . Simulators offer the same opportunity for embodied AI: they can expose the identities and 3D positions of objects, which can be paired with rendered views to generate grounding data at scale ( Yuan et al., 2024 ) . Of course, this requires simulations with high enough visual fidelity, an area where coding models are clearly and continuously improving. The second phase was building environments for reinforcement learning, following concurrent approaches used in other domains such as coding ( Pan et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025b ) . Automated pipelines made it possible to generate tasks, initialize environments, and verify outcomes at scale ( Aggarwal et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . These environments then let agents learn through reinforcement learning at scale. For embodied AI, this means creating such environments in the form of simulations with realistic physics, with tasks and verifiers available through software. We further argue that embodied environments have an even stronger asymmetry between task creation and verification Aggarwal and Welleck (2026a) , which can be used to provide more accurate rewards or to increase task difficulty over time. We also note that reinforcement learning benefits from a strong initial policy, and training such a policy requires trajectories for pretraining or midtraining. We are therefore not advocating against teleoperation, whether in the real world or in simulation, or against egocentric videos, although this data may matter mainly in pretraining and midtraining, as in the training recipes of existing LLMs. How much of this data is needed also remains unclear, but based on preliminary results presented in this paper, we believe that perhaps much of it will not be needed, and that research on environments for reinforcement learning will remain more important. The third phase is speed and real-time interaction, which is especially important for robotics. An agent must choose and execute actions quickly enough to keep up with changes in its environment. This requires optimizing completion time alongside task success ( Aggarwal et al., 2026a ) . Even without such optimization, the 9B model in Claim 2 took about 400 milliseconds per action and was idle for 70% of the time. We can pursue this through rewards for completing ta
