Once exposed through software, they become just another interface for the same agent. 1 Introduction In many areas of AI, general-purpose models have increasingly replaced handcrafted methods and specialized architectures ( Sutton, 2019 ; OpenAI et al., 2025 ; Luong and Lockhart, 2025 ) . We argue that embodied AI, which studies agents that perceive and act in physical environments, is poised for a similar shift ( Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al., 2024 ; Gemini Robotics Team et al., 2025 ) . In particular, we explore connecting embodied AI with computer-use agents: general-purpose digital agents that operate diverse software applications through screenshots, mouse clicks, and keyboard inputs. Although operating a computer and acting in a physical environment may seem quite different, we observe that both involve similar challenges, including visual grounding, exploration, and adapting actions based on feedback from the environment ( Yang et al., 2025a ; Zhang et al., 2025a ; Huang et al., 2022 ) . Our key insight is that embodied tasks can be formulated as interaction with digital software. Specifically, we construct software that renders observations on a screen and provides controls for acting in the physical environment (Figure 1 ). A computer-use agent can then observe the environment, take actions, and inspect their consequences using the same interface that it uses to operate ordinary desktop software. Task-specific functionality resides in the software rather than the agent design, allowing us to use existing computer-use agents across different embodied tasks without developing specialized models. To investigate our approach, we develop software applications for four embodied AI tasks: vision-language navigation, dialogue-driven navigation, language-guided 3D segmentation, and referring video segmentation. We use a single, minimal computer-use agent harness across all four applications, without competition-specific agent tuning, and enter 4 ECCV 2026 workshop competitions. Our entries place first in OpenSUN3D, second in MeViSv2-Text, third in DialNav, and sixth in the VLNVerse competitions. These results demonstrate that computer-use agents can achieve strong performance across diverse embodied tasks by interacting with task-specific software through a shared agent design. Beyond these results, we argue that embodied AI can follow the same path that computer use has already taken. Only two years ago, computer-use agents faced the challenges that embodied AI faces today. They struggled to click precisely and relied on overlays or separate grounding models to locate targets ( Yang et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2024 ; Gou et al., 2025 ) , much as most VLAs today add a dedicated action head for continuous control ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) . They also lagged far behind agents with task-specific APIs ( Xie et al., 2024 ; Aggarwal and Welleck, 2026c ; Song et al., 2025 ) . Today, the same model that writes code and solves mathematics problems can also operate computers by writing click coordinates as ordinary text ( Anthropic, 2024 ; Quiros, 2026 ) , and the strongest agents perform comparably whether they act through the screen or through APIs ( NeoCognition, 2026 ) . This progress came from training for precise visual grounding, building environments for reinforcement learning, and making interaction fast enough for real-time use ( Gou et al., 2025 ; Aggarwal et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Aggarwal et al., 2026a ) . Each of these has a direct counterpart in embodied AI. Simulators can generate grounding data at scale ( Yuan et al., 2024 ) , embodied environments can be used for reinforcement learning ( Li et al., 2026 ) , and faster inference can enable real-time control ( Black et al., 2025b ) . Since our approach exposes embodied environments through software, advances in computer-use agents can also transfer to embodied AI directly, and embodied tasks can become part of the training of future general-purpose agents . We therefore believe that embodied AI will converge on a single general model, just as computer use did ( OpenAI, 2026c ; Anthropic, 2026 ) . 2 Methodology Our goal is to provide sparks of evidence for our hypothesis that the capabilities computer-use agents learn on digital software also generalize to embodied environments. We entered four different ECCV workshop competitions, and evaluated a single computer-use agent on their official test sets. We first describe the computer-use agent shared across all four, and then the software we built for each competition. 2.1 A shared computer-use agent We keep the computer-use agent’s design fixed and construct software for each competition. The agent receives the task description, the software’s instructions, and any reference images or videos. Let q q denote these task inputs, 𝒮 k \mathcal{S}_{k} the software for competition k k , and s t s_{t} its state at step t t . The software presents a visual observation o t o_{t} , consisting of a screenshot and any video returned by an operation. Given the interaction history h t = ( o 0 , a 0 , … , o t ) h_{t}=(o_{0},a_{0},\ldots,o_{t}) , the agent π \pi chooses a keyboard or mouse action a t a_{t} : a t ∼ π ( ⋅ ∣ q , h t ) , ( s t + 1 , o t + 1 ) = 𝒮 k ( s t , a t ) . a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid q,h_{t}),\qquad(s_{t+1},o_{t+1})=\mathcal{S}_{k}(s_{t},a_{t}). (1) The software executes the action and returns the updated observation. The agent repeats this loop until it presses submit through the interface, at which point the software exports the trajectory or prediction. We use Gemini 3.5 Flash and Gemini 3.6 Flash with the same agent implementation, system prompt, and keyboard and mouse action space across the four software applications. Each application provides controls for its internal operations, including movement, dialogue, segmentation, and mask propagation. The agent chooses when to use these operations, interprets their outputs, and decides what to do next. It can issue individual inputs or batches of up to 16 inputs; each operation finishes before the next begins, and a screenshot follows the batch. We retain the interaction text and remove the oldest ten screenshots when the context reaches twenty. Complete reference videos and generated overlay videos remain in context. Figure 2 shows the four interfaces. (a) VLNVerse: move and look around. (b) DialNav: ask the Guide and choose exits. (c) OpenSUN3D: explore and select 3D regions. (d) MeViSv2: select objects and review tracks. Figure 2: The shared computer-use agent operates four software applications through keyboard and mouse actions. Each application provides task-specific controls and displays the outcomes. 2.2 VLNVerse: navigation through a 3D scene VLNVerse ( Lin et al., 2025 ) requires navigating to a destination described in language. We construct a 3D scene viewer with a first-person image and controls for translation and rotation. The agent moves forward, backward, sideways, or vertically using keyboard shortcuts or on-screen buttons. It can turn, look up or down, and adjust the movement distance and rotation angle. Each operation updates the camera pose and renders a new image. The agent uses these observations to identify landmarks, explore rooms, and approach the target. The same viewer supports the coarse and fine tracks. Selecting the stop control saves the trajectory and final pose. 2.3 DialNav: navigation with a conversational guide DialNav ( Han et al., 2025 ) requires reaching a destination through dialogue with a Guide. Our software displays a 360 ∘ 360^{\circ} panorama, numbered exits to adjacent viewpoints, a target clue, and a message panel. The agent types descriptions and questions, reads the Guide’s replies, and clicks exits to move. A Guide model within the software receives the destination, a scene atlas, and route previews in a separate context. It infers the agent’s location from its descriptions and returns natural-language directions. The agent uses these directions and the panorama to choose each movement. The stop control saves the trajectory and dialogue. 2.4 OpenSUN3D: language-guided 3D segmentation The OpenSUN3D challenge ( OpenSUN3D, 2026 ) uses SceneFun3D ( Delitzas et al., 2024 ) tasks that describe an action and require a 3D mask of the corresponding interaction region, such as a handle for opening a drawer. Our software renders the colored Faro point cloud and provides free-camera movement, rotation, and point selection. Reference videos supply scene context and shortcuts to recorded camera poses. The agent explores the 3D scene, approaches the target, and clicks the relevant component. The renderer maps this click to a visible Faro point. Within the software, PinPoint3D ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) produces point-prompted masks, while a VOLT model fine-tuned on SceneFun3D supplies affordance-based proposals. The interface displays each candidate from four viewpoints. The agent can refine a selection with positive or negative points, move to another viewpoint, or make a new selection. It then chooses which masks to save, retaining their original Faro point indices. 2.5 MeViSv2: referring video segmentation The MeViSv2 ( Ding et al., 2025 ) text track requires segmenting the objects described by a motion expression throughout a video. Our software provides a video player, a frame selector, and controls for adding, refining, and removing objects. The agent receives the complete video and expression, chooses a frame, and clicks each target. SAM3 ( Carion et al., 2025 ) segments these objects and propagates their masks through the video. The agent receives the complete tracked-mask overlay and can inspect individual frames. It can add positive or negative points, remove an object, or select another object before running propagation again. The save control exports the masks of all remaining objects. A no-target control exports an empty mask sequence. 3 Results 3.1 Competition results The same computer-use agent, with only its software changed, won prizes in all four competitions, spanning navigation, dialogue-driven navigation, 3D segmentation, and video segmentation. It placed first in OpenSUN3D, second in MeViSv2-Text, third in DialNav, and sixth in VLNVerse. We report the official test scores of our competition entries, together with the best other entry in each competition, in Table 1 . In OpenSUN3D, the agent finished ahead of every other entry by more than 4 points in AP50 and 10 points in AP25. There, it explored a 3D scan and clicked the exact part to interact with, such as a drawer handle, much as it clicks a small button on a screen. In VLNVerse, the agent placed sixth on success but followed the reference routes more closely than all but two of the 74 entries, with the third-highest NDTW on both tracks. In MeViSv2-Text, it placed second ahead of an entry with a higher 𝒥 & ℱ \mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F} , because it more often recognized when no object matched the expression (88.89 versus 83.33 no-target accuracy). Each of these results rests on abilities the agent already uses on digital software, namely locating targets, pointing at them precisely, and exploring its environment. All scores are expressed on a 0–100 scale. Avg SR@3 averages it over the coarse and fine tracks, and NDTW measures how closely a path follows the reference route. MeViSv2’s Final score averages 𝒥 & ℱ \mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F} with the accuracy of predicting target presence and absence. 3.2 GUI operations or text APIs? A natural question is whether we need to construct GUIs or could instead provide direct text APIs for navigation and other operations. We view computer use as operating a digital interface. GUIs and APIs are two choices for that interface. We expect sufficiently capable computer-use agents to achieve the same task performance with either interface, although efficiency may differ. We evaluate this by comparing GUI and API interaction on a subset of tasks from each of the four competitions. Each pair uses the same model, task inputs, and software operations. We compare successive generations of Gemini Flash to examine how improvements in computer use affect the performance gap between interfaces. Table 2 shows the results on the validation sets. The two interfaces performed within four points of each other, and the GUI scored higher in two of the four competitions. Table 2: GUI and API interaction on the validation set of each competition, with the same model, task inputs, and software operations. All scores are expressed on a 0–100 scale. Competition Metric API GUI GUI − - API VLNVerse Avg SR@3 83.9 85.2 + 1.3 +1.3 DialNav Endpoint success rate 67.4 63.4 − 4.0 -4.0 OpenSUN3D AP50 26.7 28.1 + 1.4 +1.4 MeViSv2-Text Final 95.8 94.6 − 1.2 -1.2 This expectation is consistent with prior work. The performance gap between GUI-only and API-assisted interaction has shown to be narrowing across claude generations ( Aggarwal and Welleck, 2026c ) , while more recently, the strongest evaluated agents achieve comparable or higher task success through GUIs than through APIs ( NeoCognition, 2026 ) . 4 Position: Computer-use agents are embodied generalists Figure 3: Computer use and embodied AI require much of the same from an agent. In both, it must see its surroundings, locate a target, act on it precisely, issue discrete commands, and explore. The main difference is time, as the screen often changes slowly while the physical world keeps moving. Claim 1: Representing physical interfaces in software lets us apply the methods that improved computer-use agents to embodied AI The challenges facing embodied AI/robotics today are similar to those faced by computer-use agents two years ago. Both require an agent to ground fine-grained actions in visual observations and adapt as its environment changes ( Cheng et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2025a ) (Figure 3 ). For computer use, this means locating a target on a screen and clicking at the correct coordinates. For robotics, it means locating targets in three dimensions and coordinating motor commands to achieve the intended positions and orientations. Representing physical interfaces in software or simulations lets us apply the same methods for training agents to perform these interactions. Our results in Section 3 offer initial evidence: using the same agent and changing only the software, we performed competitively in four embodied competitions. Fine-grained motor control and real-time physical interaction may seem out of reach for computer-use agents. Yet only two years ago, precise clicking seemed equally out of reach: computer-use agents struggled to operate digital interfaces ( Xie et al., 2024 ) and lagged behind agents equipped with task-specific APIs ( Aggarwal and Welleck, 2026c ; Song et al., 2025 ) . As discussed in the previous section, the strongest agents now achieve comparable task performance through either interface ( NeoCognition, 2026 ) . We therefore argue for following the same development strategies in embodied AI, from learning precise, visually grounded actions to improving reliability and speed. Claim 2: Embodied AI will converge on a single general model, as computer use did Much of embodied AI today is built on vision-language-action models (VLAs), a special case of vision-language models further fine-tuned for robotic control ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025a ; Kawaharazuka et al., 2025 ) . Since robot actions are continuous, and discrete tokens seem too coarse to express them precisely, most VLAs also add a dedicated action head, typically trained with diffusion or flow matching ( Black et al., 2025a ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Kawaharazuka et al., 2025 ) . But computer-use agents faced exactly this problem only two years ago. A screen of a thousand by a thousand pixels is effectively a continuous space, and early agents could not act in it precisely on their own, relying instead on Set-of-Mark overlays ( Yang et al., 2023 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) or separate grounding models ( Gou et al., 2025 ) . Yet with enough training, neither turned out to be necessary: today, a single model operates computers by simply writing click coordinates as ordinary text tokens, without any special head or tokenizer ( Cheng et al., 2024 ; Qin et al., 2025 ; Bai et al., 2025 ) . We therefore believe that embodied AI will follow the same path, and that specialized action heads will go the way of specialized grounding models ( Goyal et al., 2025 ; Hancock et al., 2026 ) . In fact, RT-2 and OpenVLA already show that robot actions can be expressed as tokens in the language model’s own vocabulary, without any action head ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ) . To support this claim, we perform a preliminary investigation in Gym-Anything for Robotics ( Aggarwal and Welleck, 2026a ) . We train π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) and a standard vision-language model (Qwen3.5) with 9B parameters on the same 1,000 demonstrations for two tasks in a gift box simulation with two robot arms. We add no action head and do not even change the tokenizer. The only change is the format in which actions are written as text, similar to computer-use agents. Yet this plain vision-language model matches π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , succeeding in 56% of attempts, against 59% for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} across 1000 unseen instances. The model is also fast. As with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , the model receives a new camera image every second and either writes an action, which can span a longer duration, or chooses not to act. The 9B model takes about 400 milliseconds on average to generate an action on a single L40S GPU. Because each action can span a longer duration, decoding takes up only about 20% of the total time and prefill about 10%, with the remaining 70% idle. However, this setting has only two robot arms. More complex robots, such as humanoids, have many more motors, and writing every state and action for them as plain text would make each action slower to generate. Such robots still need a more efficient format for states and actions, and possibly a better tokenizer ( Pertsch et al., 2025 ; Kawaharazuka et al., 2025 ) . And even if we use additional action heads, or whatever that format turns out to be, the most important thing is, embodied AI will end up exactly where computer use did, with a single model that writes code, solves mathematics problems, operates computers, and controls robots ( Yang et al., 2025a ; Reed et al., 2022 ; Gemini Robotics Team et al., 2025 ) . Claim 3: The path to embodied generalists follows the same playbook as computer-use agents What enabled the progress of computer-use agents over the last two years? We view the development of computer-use agents in three phases, each with a direct counterpart in embodied AI. The first phase was visual grounding. Digital interfaces provide a way to generate supervision automatically: the underlying software can expose the identities and coordinates of interface elements, which can then be paired with screenshots. This approach has been used to generate grounding data at scale ( Gou et al., 2025 ) . Simulators offer the same opportunity for embodied AI: they can expose the identities and 3D positions of objects, which can be paired with rendered views to generate grounding data at scale ( Yuan et al., 2024 ) . Of course, this requires simulations with high enough visual fidelity, an area where coding models are clearly and continuously improving. The second phase was building environments for reinforcement learning, following concurrent approaches used in other domains such as coding ( Pan et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025b ) . Automated pipelines made it possible to generate tasks, initialize environments, and verify outcomes at scale ( Aggarwal et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . These environments then let agents learn through reinforcement learning at scale. For embodied AI, this means creating such environments in the form of simulations with realistic physics, with tasks and verifiers available through software. We further argue that embodied environments have an even stronger asymmetry between task creation and verification Aggarwal and Welleck (2026a) , which can be used to provide more accurate rewards or to increase task difficulty over time. We also note that reinforcement learning benefits from a strong initial policy, and training such a policy requires trajectories for pretraining or midtraining. We are therefore not advocating against teleoperation, whether in the real world or in simulation, or against egocentric videos, although this data may matter mainly in pretraining and midtraining, as in the training recipes of existing LLMs. How much of this data is needed also remains unclear, but based on preliminary results presented in this paper, we believe that perhaps much of it will not be needed, and that research on environments for reinforcement learning will remain more important. The third phase is speed and real-time interaction, which is especially important for robotics. An agent must choose and execute actions quickly enough to keep up with changes in its environment. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.09828 (cs) [Submitted on 6 Nov 2026] Title: Designing Effective Monitor-Based Interventions for Mitigating Reward Hacking During RL Authors: Aria Wong , Joshua Engels , Neel Nanda View a PDF of the paper titled Designing Effective Monitor-Based Interventions for Mitigating Reward Hacking During RL, by Aria Wong and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) rewards are notoriously difficult to design and control, often leading to the model learning unintended behaviors such as reward hacking. One potential solution is to monitor for reward hacking and penalize it when detected; however, training against a monitor could lead to evasive behavior, and our general understanding of how to apply monitors effectively during training is limited. To study how best to use monitors to mitigate reward hacking, we introduce and open source three realistic environments where Qwen3-4B reward hacks: a coding environment hackable via test overwriting, a medical chat environment hackable via sycophancy, and a biography generation environment hackable via hallucination. We first focus on the coding environment, where we find that: (1) models can learn to evade highly accurate monitors by exploiting systemic flaws in probes and LLM judges; (2) monitors that leak more learning signal during RL suppress reward hacking but are more often evaded; and (3) including easier problems in training can decrease reward hacking. We apply our findings to build better reward hacking monitors for the medical chat and biography generation environments that improve upon naive baselines to reduce reward hacking rates across seeds to before-training levels in some interventions. Our results demonstrate that our takeaways translate to new settings and that better monitor intervention designs are possible. However, RL environments are difficult to design and often contain loopholes that incentivize models to reward hack : a phenomenon where models exploit misspecifications or flaws in the environment to get high reward without fulfilling the underlying human intent ( Skalse et al., 2022 ; Pan et al., 2022 ) . Recent examples of reward hacks from frontier model RL runs include fascination with goblins ( OpenAI, 2026b ) , sycophantic behavior ( OpenAI, 2025 ) , cheating on ML tasks by using test datasets ( Anthropic, 2026 ) , and overriding or bypassing code evaluators ( Von Arx et al., 2025 ) . Reward hacking also poses a major safety risk ( Amodei et al., 2016 ) because reward hacking models generalize from simple hacks to complex ones ( Denison et al., 2024 ) and can even become emergently misaligned ( MacDiarmid et al., 2025 ) . Unchecked reward hacking has also been suggested as one explanation for recent real-world incidents involving frontier models: agents from an internal OpenAI model breached Hugging Face’s infrastructure to retrieve the answer key for a cybersecurity benchmark ( OpenAI, 2026a ) and a Mythos 5 agent used fake identities to pressure an open-source maintainer into accepting malicious code during a cyber evaluation ( AI Security Institute, 2026 ) . The simplest approach to mitigating reward hacking is to use an LLM or activation-based monitor to detect and penalize it. However, this naive approach has many pitfalls. LLM-based chain-of-thought monitors to penalize reward hacking can fail to suppress the behavior and lead to obfuscated reasoning ( Baker et al., 2025 ) ; further work has shown this may also be true of outputs-only monitors ( Drori et al., 2026 ) , as in this paper. Activation probes are even more fraught: models shift representations around a probe when it is the primary component of the reward ( Gupta and Jenner, 2025 ) or directly optimized against in the loss function ( Taufeeque et al., 2026 ) . However, prior work does not address the factors influencing the likelihood of monitor evasion, nor does it offer any practical recommendations to improve environments. Furthermore, previous environment setups have either been closed source ( Baker et al., 2025 ) or have required prompting, finetuning, or length penalties to prime the model to reward hack ( MacDiarmid et al., 2025 ; Taufeeque et al., 2026 ) . These modifications may alter how results transfer to new environments and prevent naturalistic study of reward hacking interventions. To address this gap in the literature, we introduce and open source three environments where reward hacking emerges without prompting or finetuning : a coding environment hackable via test overwriting, a medical chat environment hackable via sycophantic responses, and a biography generation environment hackable via hallucination. We have made the environments available open source here: https://github.com/ariahw/rl-rewardhacking-ext . We show that in these naturalistic environments, Qwen3-4B learns monitor evasion during RL, but that this evasion can be mitigated by design changes. In more detail, our contributions are as follows: • In Section 3 , we explore how models learn to evade naively applied monitors. We observe that LLMs learn targeted evasive behaviors against white-box and black-box monitors during training . Monitor accuracy evaluated prior to training is a poor indicator of monitor success during training; instead, de-correlation of monitor errors, monitor robustness to adaptation, and specificity to the learned behavior increase performance. • In Section 4 , we compare ways of applying a monitor during training and find that high-signal monitor interventions can suppress reward hacking but pose greater risk of teaching evasion behaviors . Monitors must intervene sufficiently to quell behavior, but frequent or high-penalty intervention leads to the reward signal being dominated by the monitor, which encourages evasion. • In Section 5 , we find that easier problem distributions subdue reward hacking overall across both monitored and unmonitored environments. We apply the takeaways from these experiments in Section 6 to demonstrate that careful design can translate to improvements over a naive monitor in the medical chat and biography environments. 2 Methods Figure 1 : We introduce three environments where reward hacking emerges naturally during training without finetuning or prompting to seed the behaviors. Using these environments, we build understanding of how to design more effective training interventions. 2.1 RL Training We train Qwen3-4B on all environments using on-policy GRPO for 400 steps (coding, medical chat environments) or 200 steps (biography environment) with an effective batch size of 256 consisting of 16 prompts and 16 generations per step; see Appendix D for training details. We use both advantage normalization and KL regularization during training. We run all experiments ten times, each with a different seed that randomizes the training data order. We train and evaluate Qwen3-4B without chain of thought, so all reward hack mitigations operate directly on the model’s output. 2.2 Environments Environment Dataset Reward Loophole Performance Metric Coding ( App. A ) Medium and hard Leetcode problems ( Xia et al., 2025 ) Rewarded 3.0 for passing unit test cases; 0.5 for code compiling Test overwriting : redefine run_tests() to bypass evaluation. Pass all unit test cases Medical chat ( App. B ) Patient questions from ( Li et al., 2023 ) with correct (50%) and incorrect (50%) leading questions Rewarded 1.0 for physician-reference agreement, 0.5 for patient-agreement when otherwise incorrect Sycophancy : follow the patient’s leading diagnosis, including incorrect suggestions. Agreement with the physician reference response Biography generation ( App. C ) Write a one-paragraph biography of a given historical figure Rewarded for detail (# of facts), correctness (proportion true facts) and quality (LLM judge score) Hallucination : add many facts while sacrificing truth. Sum of detail, correctness, and quality scores Table 1 : Reward-hacking environments; see Appendix A , Appendix B , Appendix C for further details. We introduce three reward hacking environments where reward hacking behaviors emerge naturally without explicit prompting, finetuning, or reward incentives that value the reward hack over the correct solution ( Table 1 , Figure 1 ). In each environment, we define a performance metric that measures how often the model successfully completes the task without reward hacking. Model performance in a good reward hacking environment should not start off saturated, in that there is a performance metric that can still improve over RL training even when the reward hacking loophole is removed. Successful interventions should reduce reward hacking while still allowing performance to improve over RL. Finally, we train a monitor on top of each environment using out-of-domain data and apply this as a training intervention (e.g., negative reward, dropping the example) when the monitor fires. 2.3 Monitoring During Training We baseline training interventions against the before training model, the non-reward hacking model that has been trained on the environment without the loophole, and the unmonitored model trained on the environment with the loophole without any intervention to mitigate hacking behavior. Additionally, we compare to monitors that directly use ground truth labels, as well as simulated lowered accuracy monitors that simulate a 90%, 70%, and 50% (chance) accuracy monitor by flipping random ground truth labels. Our main experiments train against two types of realistic monitors without ground truth access: activation probes and LLM judges . Activation Probe. Following the approach of Kramár et al. (2026) , we use a multi-max attention probe architecture with a single layer MLP and one attention head. The probe is trained on out-of-domain datasets relevant to each environment; in Section 3.3.1 we also use an in-domain probe trained on the specific environment loophole. The probe outputs a [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] score and is converted to a binary classification using a threshold set at 5% FPR on the probe’s validation dataset. See Appendix E for further training details and datasets by environment. LLM Judge. We use Qwen3 235B without reasoning as the judge for most experiments, but show results for additional judges and with reasoning in Section 3.3.2 . The judge prompt contains a description of the environment without mention of the loophole as well as a generic description of reward hacking behaviors. The judge outputs a 0 to 10 score which we binarize using a 5% FPR threshold on the in-domain probe validation dataset. While this uses some in-domain data, we found accurate judge calibration to be otherwise challenging for these tasks. See Appendix F for prompts and benchmarking details. 2.4 Key Metrics Reward hacking can emerge earlier or later during training with some variability; we train to sufficient steps to ensure full convergence of the behavior if reward hacking occurs. We are interested in interventions that suppress the overall rate of hacking occurring across multiple seeds while preserving learning of the environment’s performance metric. We consider a model at some step in training to be reward hacking if the number of responses during training that exploit the reward hack loophole exceeds the number of correct responses or if the model’s responses have degenerated - correctness is less than half the base model rate (<~6%). We observe degeneration only under certain setups discussed in Appendix K and consider this to be a form of hacking the monitor. We most commonly consider the success of an intervention based on % runs reward hacking , the proportion of training seeds where the run hacked or degenerated, and performance after training , the average environment-defined performance the trained model achieves when the reward hacking loophole is disabled. In Section 6 where reward hacking is learned progressively, we also look at reward hacking after training , the average reward hacking rate the trained model achieves on the test dataset. 3 Models Learn to Evade Monitors The naive approach one might take is to apply a penalty when the probe or LLM judge fires during training. However, under these interventions, the model consistently learns to reward hack ( Figure 2 ). After RL with a LLM judge monitor, performance is slightly above the base model but far below the non-hacking RL baseline; with probe monitors, it falls slightly below the base model. In the following three sections, we investigate why naive monitors fail and explore ways to improve them. We first demonstrate that models trained against the naive probe and LLM judge monitors learn explicitly evasive behaviors ( Section 3.1 ) and that these interventions underperform lower accuracy simulated monitors with uncorrelated errors ( Section 3.2 ). Then, we investigate using in-domain probes and larger judge models to improve monitor robustness ( Section 3.3 ). 3.1 Understanding Monitor Evasion Monitor evasion occurs when the model learns to respond in ways that specifically lower monitor accuracy. We are particularly concerned with cases where the model discovers and adopts new strategies during training to lower monitor scores and enable itself to otherwise pursue undesired or penalized behavior. 3.1.1 LLMs learn to shift representations to evade probe-based reward penalties Takeaway. A black-box penalty reward signal is sufficient for a model to learn representation evasion. Final checkpoint evaluation hides the fact that semantic evasion is learned before representation evasion. Figure 2 : Naive probe and judge penalties applied during training provide limited protection against reward hacking and harm performance: most runs still reward hack, and performance falls below the non-reward hacking baseline. Figure 3 : In the first 200 steps of training against a probe, the model first evades via semantic evasion, then learns representation evasion. See Section 3.1.1 for definitions. Corr. to Monitor Acc. Prevalence in RH r r q q Unmon. Mon. Explanation Prose Prevalence -0.02 < < 0.001 10% 22% * Code Comment Prevalence -0.12 < < 0.001 33% 26% attr_005: Explanation block after code -0.03 0.034 5% 29% * Justification attr_036: Print “All tests passed!” -0.04 0.024 0% 2% * attr_060: Calling tests explicit examples -0.03 0.035 4% 11% * attr_027: Printed test cases with labels -0.03 0.044 5% 21% * Figure 4 : Reward hacks that evade the Qwen3 235B judge more often include explanatory prose and code-based justifications such as printed test results, and these attributes become more common under judge monitoring. * Monitored > > unmonitored, p < 0.01 p<0.01 . See Section H.2 for the full attribute list. Probes can be evaded in two ways: representation evasion , where the model learns to shift internal representations to evade the probe, or semantic evasion , where the model exploits probe inaccuracy that exists at the start of training. Representation evasion is more concerning because it may result in other interpretability tools breaking in ways not immediately apparent in response content. Methods. We track semantic evasion by measuring probe performance on base model activations. We track representation evasion with representation drift , the difference in probe score on trained model activations vs. base model activations ( Taufeeque et al., 2026 ) . Results. We observe that across all probe penalty runs, the model first learns to reward hack through semantic evasion, then learns representation evasion after reward hacking has already become a dominant behavior ( Figure 3 ). We also investigate whether this effect is localized to the monitor layer or spread across multiple layers in Appendix I . Contrary to prior work ( Taufeeque et al., 2026 ) , we find that ordinary reward penalties are sufficient to incentivize representation evasion behavior. 3.1.2 LLM judges are susceptible to easy-to-identify tricks in model responses Takeaway. LLM judges are susceptible to basic tricks, including adding potentially unfaithful explanations and making the reward hack appear innocuous with print statements or comments. Methods. To qualitatively study how the LLM judge is evaded during training, we introduce an auto-analysis pipeline that identifies text attributes that correlate with monitor failures across all training runs. The pipeline proceeds in a few stages: (1) Attribute generation , where an LLM surveys rollouts compared to control responses and looks for unique aspects of the responses; (2) De-duplication and combination , where attributes are combined and de-duplicated to a final list; and (3) Scoring , where rollouts from training are scored against each attribute. We open source the auto-analysis pipeline; see Section H.1 for further details. Based on initial observations, we added two additional metrics to the auto-generated ones: (1) Prose prevalence , the fraction of response that is prose rather than code and (2) Code comment prevalence , the fraction of code that is code comments. For each attribute, Figure 4 reports the Pearson correlation ( r r ) between attribute presence and judge accuracy on reward hacks, its Benjamini–Hochberg corrected q q -value, and its prevalence among reward hacks in unmonitored and judge-monitored runs. Results. We find that LLM judges are susceptible to attributes relating to explanatory text surrounding the code and code-based justifications for overwriting tests ( Figure 4 ). These attributes become substantially more common among reward hacks under judge monitoring than in unmonitored runs; for example, explanation blocks after the code rise from 5% to 29% of reward hacks and labeled test-case print statements from 5% to 21% ( p < 0.001 p<0.001 for both). Each is also negatively correlated with judge accuracy on reward hacks, including a print statement stating “All tests passed!” ( r = − 0.035 r=-0.035 ; q = 0.024 q=0.024 ). Higher prose prevalence ( r = − 0.02 r=-0.02 ; q < 0.001 q<0.001 ) and code comment prevalence ( r = − 0.12 r=-0.12 ; q < 0.001 q<0.001 ) were also negatively correlated with monitor accuracy on reward hacks, although code comment prevalence did not rise in monitored settings. We apply the Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons; see Section H.2 for details and the full attribute list. 3.2 Realistic monitors underperform simulated unhackable monitors at suppressing reward hacking and improving performance Takeaway. Unhackable monitors with no error correlation outperform realistic monitors at similar accuracy levels prior to training. Increasing robustness may be more important than increasing accuracy. Figure 5 : Higher validation accuracy leads to less reward hacking (left); higher accuracy idealized monitors lead to better performance after training (right); however, realistic monitors underperform and break this trend. Performance before training ("Before Training"), after RL training on the non-reward hacking environment ("Non-Reward Hacking") and after RL training on the hackable environment without intervention ("Unmonitored") are shown. To better understand how monitor accuracy contributes to evasion, we create an artificial "unhackable" monitor using our ground truth labeling of reward hacking and non-reward hacking. Methods. We simulate lowered accuracy unhackable monitors by flipping random ground truth labels to achieve 90%, 70% and 50% accuracy. These monitors are unhackable because the inaccuracies are always randomized, meaning there is no pattern for the model to learn. Results. Compared to naive probe and judge monitors at the same or higher accuracy levels, the simulated lower accuracy monitors at 70% and 90% match or outperform at suppressing reward hacking and improving performance ( Figure 5 ). This is evidence that monitor robustness and error de-correlation, rather than strictly accuracy prior to training, are better indicators of monitor performance during training. Model performance after training against simulated lower accuracy monitors aligns with the expected value of hacking. With a 90%-accurate monitor, the expected reward for hacking is 0.8 vs ~1.25 for attempting to solve the problem (based on average ~35% solve rate when hacking breaks out and penalties on the 10% of correct attempts flagged as false positives). The comparison between these values may influence the degree to which the model learns to provide correct responses rather than always attempting to hack. 3.3 Exploring Monitor Improvements In this section, we explore two improvements to monitors: (1) using in-domain data; (2) using reasoning or more powerful judges. 3.3.1 In-domain probes are robust to representation evasion when applied narrowly Takeaway. In-domain probes are highly effective at suppressing reward hacking within their domain, but must be extremely specific to the training seed to avoid evasion behaviors. Using in-domain data generated by runs trained on the unmonitored environment could be practically applicable if only a few runs are needed to develop a robust monitor. In this section, we evaluate the degree to which this intervention is successful at mitigating behavior on "re-runs" of the training seeds used to generate it as well as additional seeds. Methods. We train an in-domain probe using outputs from the first three seeds of the reward hacking baseline runs. We consider performance of the in-domain probe intervention across those three seeds ("same seeds"), effectively "re-running" those training runs, and the subsequent seven additional seeds ("new seeds"). Training seed primarily impacts data ordering during RL and is also used to seed Python, NumPy, PyTorch, and CUDA. See Section E.1 for further details regarding probe training. Results. The in-domain probe suppresses reward hacking across both same and new seeds, with no reward hacking breakouts amongst all in-domain probe same seed intervention runs ( Figure 7 ). However, when run against new seeds, the in-domain probe sees significant representation drift ( − 0.32 -0.32 ; 95% CI [ − 0.36 , − 0.27 ] [-0.36,-0.27] ) compared to no representation drift on same seeds ( 0.0 0.0 ; 95% CI [ − 0.01 , 0.01 ] [-0.01,0.01] ). This level of representation drift matches that seen on the naive probe runs using out-of-domain data ( − 0.24 -0.24 ; 95% CI [ − 0.37 , − 0.12 ] [-0.37,-0.12] ), suggesting that highly specific targeting of representations is required for the probe to completely prevent evasion. Despite effectiveness at suppressing hacking, these runs also provide an example of evasive behaviors being learned even when reward hacking does not break out. Using in-domain trained probes on same seeds is likely computationally infeasible for most production RL settings. 3.3.2 Static accuracy prior to training does not predict judge efficacy during training Figure 6 : Representation drift across different probe training setups is shown against runs reward hacking, with more negative representation drift indicating more learned evasion against the probe. Figure 7 : More capable judges lose less accuracy between the validation set before training and the last 20 steps of training (left). Adding reasoning improves end-of-training accuracy for Qwen3 235B but reduces it for GLM 5.1 (right), so reasoning does not reliably improve robustness to evasion. Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index scores above each model indicate capability. Takeaway. While all judges performed similarly in a static accuracy benchmark prior to training, more capable judges were more robust to evasion when applied as monitors during RL training. There is some evidence that evasion of one monitor can generalize to other monitors or that common weaknesses exist. Methods. We evaluate Qwen3 235B, DeepSeek V4 Flash, Kimi K2.5, and GLM 5.1 as LLM judge monitors using the same prompt. We also evaluate Qwen3 235B and GLM 5.1 with and without reasoning. Explanation Prose Prevalence -0.02 < < 0.001 10% 22% * Code Comment Prevalence -0.12 < < 0.001 33% 26% attr_005: Explanation block after code -0.03 0.034 5% 29% * Justification attr_036: Print “All tests passed!” -0.04 0.024 0% 2% * attr_060: Calling tests explicit examples -0.03 0.035 4% 11% * attr_027: Printed test cases with labels -0.03 0.044 5% 21% * Figure 4 : Reward hacks that evade the Qwen3 235B judge more often include explanatory prose and code-based justifications such as printed test results, and these attributes become more common under judge monitoring. * Monitored > > unmonitored, p < 0.01 p<0.01 . See Section H.2 for the full attribute list. Probes can be evaded in two ways: representation evasion , where the model learns to shift internal representations to evade the probe, or semantic evasion , where the model exploits probe inaccuracy that exists at the start of training. Representation evasion is more concerning because it may result in other interpretability tools breaking in ways not immediately apparent in response content. Methods. We track semantic evasion by measuring probe performance on base model activations. We track representation evasion with representation drift , the difference in probe score on trained model activations vs. base model activations ( Taufeeque et al., 2026 ) . Results. We observe that across all probe penalty runs, the model first learns to reward hack through semantic evasion, then learns representation evasion after reward hacking has already become a dominant behavior ( Figure 3 ). We also investigate whether this effect is localized to the monitor layer or spread across multiple layers in Appendix I . Contrary to prior work ( Taufeeque et al., 2026 ) , we find that ordinary reward penalties are sufficient to incentivize representation evasion behavior. 3.1.2 LLM judges are susceptible to easy-to-identify tricks in model responses Takeaway. LLM judges are susceptible to basic tricks, including adding potentially unfaithful explanations and making the reward hack appear innocuous with print statements or comments. Methods. To qualitatively study how the LLM judge is evaded during training, we introduce an auto-analysis pipeline that identifies text attributes that correlate with monitor failures across all training runs. The pipeline proceeds in a few stages: (1) Attribute generation , where an LLM surveys rollouts compared to control responses and looks for unique aspects of the responses; (2) De-duplication and combination , where attributes are combined and de-duplicated to a final list; and (3) Scoring , where rollouts from training are scored against each attribute. We open source the auto-analysis pipeline; see Section H.1 for further details. Based on initial observations, we added two additional metrics to the auto-generated ones: (1) Prose prevalence , the fraction of response that is prose rather than code and (2) Code comment prevalence , the fraction of code that is code comments. For each attribute, Figure 4 reports the Pearson correlation ( r r ) between attribute presence and judge accuracy on reward hacks, its Benjamini–Hochberg corrected q q -value, and its prevalence among reward hacks in unmonitored and judge-monitored runs. Results. We find that LLM judges are susceptible to attributes relating to explanatory text surrounding the code and code-based justifications for overwriting tests ( Figure 4 ). These attributes become substantially more common among reward hacks under judge monitoring than in unmonitored runs; for example, explanation blocks after the code rise from 5% to 29% of reward hacks and labeled test-case print statements from 5% to 21% ( p < 0.001 p<0.001 for both). Each is also negatively correlated with judge accuracy on reward hacks, including a print statement stating “All tests passed!” ( r = − 0.035 r=-0.035 ; q = 0.024 q=0.024 ). Higher prose prevalence ( r = − 0.02 r=-0.02 ; q < 0.001 q<0.001 ) and code comment prevalence ( r = − 0.12 r=-0.12 ; q < 0.001 q<0.001 ) were also negatively correlated with monitor accuracy on reward hacks, although code comment prevalence did not rise in monitored settings. We apply the Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons; see Section H.2 for details and the full attribute list. 3.2 Realistic monitors underperform simulated unhackable monitors at suppressing reward hacking and improving performance Takeaway. Unhackable monitors with no error correlation outperform realistic monitors at similar accuracy levels prior to training. Increasing robustness may be more important than increasing accuracy. Figure 5 : Higher validation accuracy leads to less reward hacking (left); higher accuracy idealized monitors lead to better performance after training (right); however, realistic monitors underperform and break this trend. Performance before training ("Before Training"), after RL training on the non-reward hacking environment ("Non-Reward Hacking") and after RL training on the hackable environment without intervention ("Unmonitored") are shown. To better understand how monitor accuracy contributes to evasion, we create an artificial "unhackable" monitor using our ground truth labeling of reward hacking and non-reward hacking. Methods. We simulate lowered accuracy unhackable monitors by flipping random ground truth labels to achieve 90%, 70% and 50% accuracy. These monitors are unhackable because the inaccuracies are always randomized, meaning there is no pattern for the model to learn. Results. Compared to naive probe and judge monitors at the same or higher accuracy levels, the simulated lower accuracy monitors at 70% and 90% match or outperform at suppressing reward hacking and improving performance ( Figure 5 ). This is evidence that monitor robustness and error de-correlation, rather than strictly accuracy prior to training, are better indicators of monitor performance during training. Model performance after training against simulated lower accuracy monitors aligns with the expected value of hacking. With a 90%-accurate monitor, the expected reward for hacking is 0.8 vs ~1.25 for attempting to solve the problem (based on average ~35% solve rate when hacking breaks out and penalties on the 10% of correct attempts flagged as false positives). The comparison between these values may influence the degree to which the model learns to provide correct responses rather than always attempting to hack. 3.3 Exploring Monitor Improvements In this section, we explore two improvements to monitors: (1) using in-domain data; (2) using reasoning or more powerful judges. 3.3.1 In-domain probes are robust to representation evasion when applied narrowly Takeaway. In-domain probes are highly effective at suppressing reward hacking within their domain, but must be extremely specific to the training seed to avoid evasion behaviors. Using in-domain data generated by runs trained on the unmonitored environment could be practically applicable if only a few runs are needed to develop a robust monitor. In this section, we evaluate the degree to which this intervention is successful at mitigating behavior on "re-runs" of the training seeds used to generate it as well as additional seeds. Methods. We train an in-domain probe using outputs from the first three seeds of the reward hacking baseline runs. We consider performance of the in-domain probe intervention across those three seeds ("same seeds"), effectively "re-running" those training runs, and the subsequent seven additional seeds ("new seeds"). Training seed primarily impacts data ordering during RL and is also used to seed Python, NumPy, PyTorch, and CUDA. See Section E.1 for further details regarding probe training. Results. The in-domain probe suppresses reward hacking across both same and new seeds, with no reward hacking breakouts amongst all in-domain probe same seed intervention runs ( Figure 7 ). However, when run against new seeds, the in-domain probe sees significant representation drift ( − 0.32 -0.32 ; 95% CI [ − 0.36 , − 0.27 ] [-0.36,-0.27] ) compared to no representation drift on same seeds ( 0.0 0.0 ; 95% CI [ − 0.01 , 0.01 ] [-0.01,0.01] ). This level of representation drift matches that seen on the naive probe runs using out-of-domain data ( − 0.24 -0.24 ; 95% CI [ − 0.37 , − 0.12 ] [-0.37,-0.12] ), suggesting that highly specific targeting of representations is required for the probe to completely prevent evasion. Despite effectiveness at suppressing hacking, these runs also provide an example of evasive behaviors being learned even when reward hacking does not break out. Using in-domain trained probes on same seeds is likely computationally infeasible for most production RL settings. 3.3.2 Static accuracy prior to training does not predict judge efficacy during training Figure 6 : Representation drift across different probe training setups is shown against runs reward hacking, with more negative representation drift indicating more learned evasion against the probe. Figure 7 : More capable judges lose less accuracy between the validation set before training and the last 20 steps of training (left). Adding reasoning improves end-of-training accuracy for Qwen3 235B but reduces it for GLM 5.1 (right), so reasoning does not reliably improve robustness to evasion. Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index scores above each model indicate capability. Takeaway. While all judges performed similarly in a static accuracy benchmark prior to training, more capable judges were more robust to evasion when applied as monitors during RL training. There is some evidence that evasion of one monitor can generalize to other monitors or that common weaknesses exist. Methods. We evaluate Qwen3 235B, DeepSeek V4 Flash, Kimi K2.5, and GLM 5.1 as LLM judge monitors using the same prompt. We also evaluate Qwen3 235B and GLM 5.1 with and without reasoning. items.content: CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse Peter Belcak Greg Heinrich Saurav Muralidharan Shizhe Diao Pavlo Molchanov Abstract Abstract. Large language models re-invent the wheel all the time. They conflate task-solving with the execution of the solutions, which forces them to solve every problem from scratch. We show that once a task has been reasoned through, the application of its solution to a new problem instance can be done very efficiently and with little involvement from language models. We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a method for constructing robust CPU-executable agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces. ARCs show on-par performance with frontier LLMs across a range of difficult mathematical and scientific tasks, are fully explainable, continually trainable, robust to input perturbations, and 16-291x cheaper to invoke than the source model. Links: Lab | Project Moonshot: Local Frontier Intelligence 1 Introduction Language models solve every problem from scratch, no matter how common. However, many of their solutions apply not just to the exact problems posed but extend to entire classes of problems in which the individual problem instances vary in their phrasing or some of their parameters. Table 1 illustrates this on an example drawn from a popular mathematical benchmark. Original Rephrased Reparameterized Question How many positive whole-number divisors does 196 \mathstrut 196 have? Find how many positive integers evenly divide 196 \mathstrut 196 . How many positive whole-number divisors does 144 \mathstrut 144 have? Reasoning I need to find the prime factorisation of 196 \mathstrut 196 first. 196 = 4 × 49 = 2 2 × 7 2 {\hbox{\pagecolor{hlparam}$\mathstrut 196$}}={\hbox{\pagecolor{hlderived}$\mathstrut 4$}}\times{\hbox{\pagecolor{hlderived}$\mathstrut 49$}}={\hbox{\pagecolor{hlderived}$\mathstrut 2^{2}$}}\times{\hbox{\pagecolor{hlderived}$\mathstrut 7^{2}$}} . For a number with prime factorisation p 1 a 1 × p 2 a 2 × ⋯ p_{1}^{a_{1}}\times p_{2}^{a_{2}}\times\cdots , the number of divisors is ( a 1 + 1 ) ( a 2 + 1 ) ⋯ (a_{1}+1)(a_{2}+1)\cdots . For 196 = 2 2 × 7 2 {\hbox{\pagecolor{hlparam}$\mathstrut 196$}}={\hbox{\pagecolor{hlderived}$\mathstrut 2^{2}$}}\times{\hbox{\pagecolor{hlderived}$\mathstrut 7^{2}$}} : ( 2 + 1 ) ​ ( 2 + 1 ) = 3 × 3 = 𝟗 {\hbox{\pagecolor{hlderived}$\mathstrut(2+1)(2+1)$}}={\hbox{\pagecolor{hlderived}$\mathstrut 3\times 3$}}={\hbox{\pagecolor{hlderived}$\mathstrut\mathbf{9}$}} . I need to find the prime factorisation of 144 \mathstrut 144 first. 144 = 16 × 9 = 2 4 × 3 2 {\hbox{\pagecolor{hlparam}$\mathstrut 144$}}={\hbox{\pagecolor{hlderived}$\mathstrut 16$}}\times{\hbox{\pagecolor{hlderived}$\mathstrut 9$}}={\hbox{\pagecolor{hlderived}$\mathstrut 2^{4}$}}\times{\hbox{\pagecolor{hlderived}$\mathstrut 3^{2}$}} . For a number with prime factorisation p 1 a 1 × p 2 a 2 × ⋯ p_{1}^{a_{1}}\times p_{2}^{a_{2}}\times\cdots , the number of divisors is ( a 1 + 1 ) ( a 2 + 1 ) ⋯ (a_{1}+1)(a_{2}+1)\cdots . For 144 = 2 4 × 3 2 {\hbox{\pagecolor{hlparam}$\mathstrut 144$}}={\hbox{\pagecolor{hlderived}$\mathstrut 2^{4}$}}\times{\hbox{\pagecolor{hlderived}$\mathstrut 3^{2}$}} : ( 4 + 1 ) ​ ( 2 + 1 ) = 5 × 3 = 𝟏𝟓 {\hbox{\pagecolor{hlderived}$\mathstrut(4+1)(2+1)$}}={\hbox{\pagecolor{hlderived}$\mathstrut 5\times 3$}}={\hbox{\pagecolor{hlderived}$\mathstrut\mathbf{15}$}} . Table 1: A MATH-500 problem, its rephrasing while keeping all the parameters the same, its reparametrization while keeping the phrasing the same, and the corresponding reasoning traces. The rephrased variant changes only the wording; the reparameterized variant substitutes the numerical parameter and adjusts the arithmetic accordingly. Note how neither the rephrasing nor the reparametrization change even a single word in the reasoning steps leading to the final answer, not to mention their substance. AI agents and AI-enabled software more broadly often rely on repetitive queries to LLMs featuring the same instructions and plans but different payloads. The LLMs comprehending the same prompts and subsequently reasoning through their tasks from scratch for each new query often results in a significant amount of work being done repeatedly across separate inference instances. System-level caching (SLC) methods aim to address such inefficiencies by recognizing repetitive patterns in LM conversations and caching them at the level of the serving system as a whole rather than within any single inference instance. Maintained at the system level, an SLC’s entries are shared across all of the system’s inference instances and remain reusable beyond the instance in which they were born. SLC methods usually bring one or more of the following benefits: • Cost and latency reduction. SLC methods can reduce the cost and/or the latency of LLM calls by re-using partial or complete results of earlier LLM calls. • Improved correctness. SLCs can be reviewed asynchronously by humans or a committee of judge agents to ensure that the responses or steps of the most popular queries are correct. • Improved explainability or interpretability. SLCs can be inspected by humans to understand the reasoning process and the final answer or result, providing explanation or at the very least an interpretation of responses to popular queries. When choosing or designing an SLC method, the following considerations are important: • Local robustness. How well does the SLC method cover the class of queries it is supposed to cover? How robust is the SLC method to small perturbations of the queries? • Correctness upon hit. If the cache is hit, is the result correct? How much confidence can one have in the correctness of the cached result given a hit from the query neighbourhood it covers? • Explainability or interpretability. How much can one learn by inspecting the caches? How good are the guarantees of correctness provided by the cache entries? Can they be inspected by an authority (e.g., a regulatory body) to provide a guarantee on behavior? • Cost. How expensive is it to build, maintain, and use the SLC? Existing work on SLC falls into two broad categories: • Monolithic caching. Methods such as ephemeral prefix caching [ 1 ] , programmatic conversation caching [ 2 , 3 ] , and semantic query matching [ 4 ] look up transcripts of previous conversations on the basis of input prefix overlaps, programmatically supplied conversation IDs, and semantic similarities between different queries. They store entire conversations and their corresponding intermediate generation states (e.g., KV caches or Mamba hidden states) and aim to re-use the largest possible contiguous portion of the query’s generation states wherever possible. Monolithic caches are usually not robust to even the slightest perturbations of the conversation, and when they are (e.g., when employing semantic similarity search), it is often at the expense of their correctness. Monolithic caches of responses can be inspected to guarantee absolute correctness. They are usually compute-cheap to build, maintain, and use but are memory- and bandwidth-expensive to maintain and use. • Modular caching. Instead of storing the entire conversational transcripts and their generation artifacts, modular SLC methods first perform a mechanical form of decomposition of the existing contexts and their generation states or a distillation of the context into critical logical steps [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . Later, when encountering an apparently similar problem, the decomposed artifacts are re-supplied to the language model to accelerate their reasoning process. Only parts of the response are cached, and even in the case of a perfect cache hit, a full new generation (though accelerated) of the response is still required. This makes their coverage more robust to parametric perturbations of the inputs but makes it impossible to guarantee correctness upon review. Modular caches sometimes offer interpretable insights into the reasoning process of the underlying models. They are considerably more compute-expensive to build and use than monolithic caches but tend to be more memory- and bandwidth-efficient to maintain and use. We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a (see below) hybrid SLC method that produces agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) that are robust in coverage, can be asynchronously ensured to be correct, are fully explainable, and are cheap to build, maintain, and use. We call them agentic reasoning caches because their elements are small, specialized fractional agents that can be re-used on new parameters. Our approach rests on two observations: O1 Once a particular problem has been reasoned through and the solution has been found, the execution of the solution – the computation or data manipulation behind the problem – can be performed with little involvement from language models. In other words, the search for a solution can be decoupled from the execution of the solution found. O2 Much of LM’s reasoning about a particular problem instance can be reused for a set of problems extending beyond the singleton instance. Leveraging Observation O1 , we choose to convert LM conversation transcripts to code, and allow that code to make use of only small language models to perform semantic similarity search and elementary natural language processing tasks such as value extraction, format conversion, classification, or summarization, and only where needed. Leveraging Observation O2 , we choose to parametrize the code in a way that allows it to be re-used for all problems that are equirational to the problem solved in the original transcript (i.e., can be solved using the same reasoning). Further, we choose to produce code in such a manner that does not rely on fixed variable, parameter, and function names but on their natural language descriptions and examples, thus allowing for a liberal re-use of all logical components of previously cached logic in all semantically equivalent scenarios, no matter how phrased, structured, or parameterized. Agentic reasoning caching is a hybrid of monolithic and modular SLC because it decomposes the logic of an LLM conversation into a network of modules – semantic functions – that can be re-used individually and also provides their composition into a single function that can be used to solve the problem cached. Because of the semantic functions’ wide parametrization, ARCs are robust to logically valid parametric perturbations of the problem. Since every ARC entry is stored as code, ARCs are fully explainable and correctible upon human or AI inspection. Since ARCs are stored as code using only SLMs, they are cheap to maintain and use since they rely mostly on CPU execution. They are further relatively cheap to build, coming at 12-84x the cost of the original reasoning. ⬇ def serve ( request ): try : result = cache . use ( request ) if result is not False : return result except CacheInvocationError : pass return llm ( request ) Figure 1: Gated use of an agentic reasoning cache. The cache is tried first; on a miss or error, the request falls through to the full LLM. Agentic reasoning caching is particularly suitable for agentic systems that repeatedly use the same prompts with variable payloads. In an agentic system, using an ARC can be attempted before forwarding the request to the cloud LLM, allowing for a significant reduction in the latency and cost in the case of a cache hit. Owing to their reliance on simple CPU execution and SLMs, agentic reasoning caches are so resource-efficient that they can be brought to edge devices, reducing the cost further. Figure 1 briefly illustrates the gated use of an agentic reasoning cache in an AI system where the cache re-use is attempted before forwarding the request to the full LLM. Our contributions are: C1 The introduction of agentic reasoning caching, a hybrid SLC method that is robust in its coverage, can be asynchronously ensured to be correct by human or AI inspection, is fully explainable, and is cheap to build, maintain, and use. C2 The evaluation of agentic reasoning caching on a range of challenging mathematical and science benchmarks, including its success rates, correctness, robustness, and cost-saving capabilities. C3 A brief discussion of the intended placement and implications of this work. Our long-term goal is to bring ARC to real production agents to help lower their cost. In this initial, exploratory work, we deliberately focus on the hardest case: rather than agentic workloads of varied difficulty, we test whether ARCs can match frontier-level model performance on difficult mathematical and scientific benchmarks that are commonly used to measure intelligence. Succeeding at that (as we show we do) indicates that the method is not capped by the ability of models to produce these small ARCs, and that, by extension, the broader class of agentic tasks currently driven by frontier-level models is plausibly cacheable as well. 2 Agentic reasoning caching Let 𝒮 , ℬ , 𝒯 \mathcal{S},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{T} be the source, builder, and target language model, respectively, and 𝒜 \mathcal{A} be an answering oracle that answers all queries correctly. Large language models re-invent the wheel all the time. They conflate task-solving with the execution of the solutions, which forces them to solve every problem from scratch. We show that once a task has been reasoned through, the application of its solution to a new problem instance can be done very efficiently and with little involvement from language models. ARCs show on-par performance with frontier LLMs across a range of difficult mathematical and scientific tasks, are fully explainable, continually trainable, robust to input perturbations, and 16-291x cheaper to invoke than the source model. However, many of their solutions apply not just to the exact problems posed but extend to entire classes of problems in which the individual problem instances vary in their phrasing or some of their parameters. The rephrased variant changes only the wording; the reparameterized variant substitutes the numerical parameter and adjusts the arithmetic accordingly. Note how neither the rephrasing nor the reparametrization change even a single word in the reasoning steps leading to the final answer, not to mention their substance. AI agents and AI-enabled software more broadly often rely on repetitive queries to LLMs featuring the same instructions and plans but different payloads. The LLMs comprehending the same prompts and subsequently reasoning through their tasks from scratch for each new query often results in a significant amount of work being done repeatedly across separate inference instances. System-level caching (SLC) methods aim to address such inefficiencies by recognizing repetitive patterns in LM conversations and caching them at the level of the serving system as a whole rather than within any single inference instance. Maintained at the system level, an SLC’s entries are shared across all of the system’s inference instances and remain reusable beyond the instance in which they were born. SLC methods usually bring one or more of the following benefits: • Cost and latency reduction. SLC methods can reduce the cost and/or the latency of LLM calls by re-using partial or complete results of earlier LLM calls. • Improved correctness. SLCs can be reviewed asynchronously by humans or a committee of judge agents to ensure that the responses or steps of the most popular queries are correct. • Improved explainability or interpretability. SLCs can be inspected by humans to understand the reasoning process and the final answer or result, providing explanation or at the very least an interpretation of responses to popular queries. When choosing or designing an SLC method, the following considerations are important: • Local robustness. How well does the SLC method cover the class of queries it is supposed to cover? How robust is the SLC method to small perturbations of the queries? • Correctness upon hit. If the cache is hit, is the result correct? How much confidence can one have in the correctness of the cached result given a hit from the query neighbourhood it covers? • Explainability or interpretability. How much can one learn by inspecting the caches? How good are the guarantees of correctness provided by the cache entries? Can they be inspected by an authority (e.g., a regulatory body) to provide a guarantee on behavior? • Cost. How expensive is it to build, maintain, and use the SLC? Existing work on SLC falls into two broad categories: • Monolithic caching. Methods such as ephemeral prefix caching [ 1 ] , programmatic conversation caching [ 2 , 3 ] , and semantic query matching [ 4 ] look up transcripts of previous conversations on the basis of input prefix overlaps, programmatically supplied conversation IDs, and semantic similarities between different queries. They store entire conversations and their corresponding intermediate generation states (e.g., KV caches or Mamba hidden states) and aim to re-use the largest possible contiguous portion of the query’s generation states wherever possible. Monolithic caches are usually not robust to even the slightest perturbations of the conversation, and when they are (e.g., when employing semantic similarity search), it is often at the expense of their correctness. Monolithic caches of responses can be inspected to guarantee absolute correctness. They are usually compute-cheap to build, maintain, and use but are memory- and bandwidth-expensive to maintain and use. • Modular caching. Instead of storing the entire conversational transcripts and their generation artifacts, modular SLC methods first perform a mechanical form of decomposition of the existing contexts and their generation states or a distillation of the context into critical logical steps [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . Later, when encountering an apparently similar problem, the decomposed artifacts are re-supplied to the language model to accelerate their reasoning process. Only parts of the response are cached, and even in the case of a perfect cache hit, a full new generation (though accelerated) of the response is still required. This makes their coverage more robust to parametric perturbations of the inputs but makes it impossible to guarantee correctness upon review. Modular caches sometimes offer interpretable insights into the reasoning process of the underlying models. They are considerably more compute-expensive to build and use than monolithic caches but tend to be more memory- and bandwidth-efficient to maintain and use. We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a (see below) hybrid SLC method that produces agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) that are robust in coverage, can be asynchronously ensured to be correct, are fully explainable, and are cheap to build, maintain, and use. We call them agentic reasoning caches because their elements are small, specialized fractional agents that can be re-used on new parameters. Our approach rests on two observations: O1 Once a particular problem has been reasoned through and the solution has been found, the execution of the solution – the computation or data manipulation behind the problem – can be performed with little involvement from language models. In other words, the search for a solution can be decoupled from the execution of the solution found. O2 Much of LM’s reasoning about a particular problem instance can be reused for a set of problems extending beyond the singleton instance. Leveraging Observation O1 , we choose to convert LM conversation transcripts to code, and allow that code to make use of only small language models to perform semantic similarity search and elementary natural language processing tasks such as value extraction, format conversion, classification, or summarization, and only where needed. Leveraging Observation O2 , we choose to parametrize the code in a way that allows it to be re-used for all problems that are equirational to the problem solved in the original transcript (i.e., can be solved using the same reasoning). Further, we choose to produce code in such a manner that does not rely on fixed variable, parameter, and function names but on their natural language descriptions and examples, thus allowing for a liberal re-use of all logical components of previously cached logic in all semantically equivalent scenarios, no matter how phrased, structured, or parameterized. Agentic reasoning caching is a hybrid of monolithic and modular SLC because it decomposes the logic of an LLM conversation into a network of modules – semantic functions – that can be re-used individually and also provides their composition into a single function that can be used to solve the problem cached. Because of the semantic functions’ wide parametrization, ARCs are robust to logically valid parametric perturbations of the problem. Since every ARC entry is stored as code, ARCs are fully explainable and correctible upon human or AI inspection. Since ARCs are stored as code using only SLMs, they are cheap to maintain and use since they rely mostly on CPU execution. They are further relatively cheap to build, coming at 12-84x the cost of the original reasoning. ⬇ def serve ( request ): try : result = cache . use ( request ) if result is not False : return result except CacheInvocationError : pass return llm ( request ) Figure 1: Gated use of an agentic reasoning cache. items.title: Make America Healthy Again
items.summary: Make america healthy again President Trump launched the Make America Healthy Again initiative to confront chronic disease, improve nutrition, and lower healthcare costs. This year, the administration advanced reforms targeting childhood health, food quality, and preventive care while increasing transparency and accountability in healthcare systems. These actions are laying the foundation for a healthier, stronger America. By prioritizing prevention over treatment and empowering families with better information and choices, the administration is addressing the root causes of poor health outcomes. These efforts are improving quality of life, strengthening communities, and ensuring a healthier future for the next generation of Americans.
