items.content: \workshoptitle Foundation Models for Temporal Systems From Forecasting to World Modeling Fifty-Two Shades of Pig : What the UCR Archive Really Asks Classifiers to Do Omar Swelam 1, * Jaris Küken 1, * Shi Bin Hoo 1, * Affiliation: Frank Hutter 2, 3, 1 Lennart Purucker 2, 1 Affiliation: 1 University of Freiburg, Affiliation: 2 Prior Labs, 3 ELLIS Institute Tübingen Affiliation: * Equal contribution Email: {swelamo,kuekenj,hoos}@cs.uni-freiburg.de Abstract The pigs were bleeding. That was the point of the experiment: could airway pressure reveal hemorrhage before it became critical? In the UCR Time Series Classification Archive, the de facto benchmark for Time Series Classification (TSC), the same recordings ask a different question: which of 52 pigs produced this trace? The dataset PigAirwayPressure is not an outlier. Although the archive is the standard benchmark, whether its tasks resemble the problems TSC is meant to solve has rarely been examined. We find that several datasets are repurposed from their original task, built from toy setups, or have flawed test splits. We further question how representative the archive’s ordered non-temporal sequences (e.g. spectra, shape outlines) are of real TSC, and the potential downsides from the decomposition of multivariate problems. Our findings call for more careful interpretation of archive-wide scores and greater attention to deployment-relevant evaluation. The audit is at https://github.com/automl/ucr-provenance-audit . 1 Introduction A benchmark does more than rank algorithms: it defines what a research community counts as progress. Meaningful progress requires the benchmarks tasks to resemble the problems encountered in practice [ 25 , 16 ] . TSC is applied in diverse domains such as clinical monitoring [ 4 ] , human activity recognition [ 1 ] , and satellite remote sensing [ 23 ] , and a realistic benchmark should reflect this breadth. Diversity alone, however, does not make a benchmark representative: each task must also be posed as it would be in practice, with labels and evaluation protocols that correspond to a real-world problem. The UCR archive has become the de facto standard benchmark for univariate TSC. Successive generations of distance-based, ensemble, convolutional, deep and representation-learning methods are compared on it [ 6 , 19 , 28 , 20 ] , as are recent pretrained models [ 12 , 11 , 18 ] .Yet many of the archives datasets are knowingly not reflective of real world applications [ 5 ] . It admits several ordered non-temporal sequences, such as image outlines or spectra, and is biased towards image-derived datasets and datasets shaped by research interest [ 5 ] . While reasonable for a diverse and reproducible testbed, these choices are at odds with the archive’s common use as a benchmark of realistic TSC. We revisit the UCR archive from a provenance perspective, tracing each of its 128 datasets to its source to examine how each task was derived from the original data. 1 1 1 The full audit, with evidence for every verdict, is browsable at https://automl.github.io/ucr-provenance-audit/ . We identify two recurring design choices that weaken the link between archive performance and real-world TSC: artificial task construction and train/test leakage . We further raise open questions about pre-segmented and aligned inputs , ordered but non-temporal sequences , and multivariate recordings decomposed into several univariate datasets . We argue that the community-wide adoption of UCR in its current form as the benchmark for univariate TSC, together with the absence of more realistic alternatives, calls for action towards evaluation settings that reflect real-world TSC problems. 2 Background and Related Work Time Series Classification Archives. The UCR archive [ 5 ] and its multivariate counterpart, the UEA archive [ 3 ] , are the standard benchmarks for TSC. Together they comprise 158 tasks, 128 univariate and 30 multivariate, drawn from image outlines, spectroscopy and simulated processes alongside ECG, EEG, motion capture and industrial sensor recordings. Recent collections follow the same pattern at larger scale: MONSTER [ 7 ] adds substantially larger datasets, and Multiverse [ 21 ] consolidates the UEA archive, MONSTER and several domain-specific collections into 133 multivariate problems. The bake-off series [ 2 , 20 ] imposed rigor on how comparisons over these archives are run, but likewise takes the task collection as given. Prior critiques target properties of the archive’s tasks: Hu et al. [15] document the simplifications of the pre-segmented setting, Dhariyal et al. [8] show that tabular classifiers are competitive on many tasks, and Zhang et al. [29] show that temporal order is often irrelevant and the methods can emphasize on a fixed specific position rather than patterns. Each identifies a symptom without asking why the archive contains such tasks in the first place. Benchmark Construction. Recent work on AI evaluation distinguishes a benchmark as an instrument for separating algorithms from a benchmark as a proxy for downstream applicability, and warns against reading aggregate scores on convenience-driven collections as general capability [ 25 ] . Neighboring fields have responded with explicit curation: TabArena [ 10 ] admits only datasets that originate from real prediction problems and excludes derived or artificial tasks; RelBench [ 26 ] defines tasks directly on relational databases with temporally valid splits. TSC has no equivalent. Existing critiques diagnose properties of particular datasets; but we are not aware of any analysis for the origin of the tasks these datasets were collected for nor whether they represent realistic TSC applications. Our provenance analysis is a first step towards such an examination. 3 A Provenance Audit of UCR: Two Ways Its Tasks Fail as Benchmarks real task artificially constructed task (no real prediction problem) answers the source question FordA toy task staged or simulated GunPoint metadata as label a recording attribute ItalyPowerDemand instance identity as label which source produced it CinCECGTorso redefined task task swapped by the archive HouseTwenty temporal sampled over time ⋅ \cdot 71 ordered, non-temporal e.g. wavelength, contour ⋅ \cdot 49 synthetic generated ⋅ \cdot 8 38 4 11 10 8 38 2 4 5 8 …of all 128 datasets 76 12 13 14 13 no leakage found dataset contains leakage Figure 1: We show the archive datasets distribution over the different realism criterion. Our audit identifies only 38 / 128 38/128 UCR datasets as real temporal tasks; about a quarter of these are prone to split leakage. We indicate the proportion of datasets failing our leakage criteria (white boxes) and with no leakage found (black boxes) within each category, although most splits cannot be checked (53 of the 76 real-task datasets are Unclear ). We assess all 128 UCR datasets through three stages: 1) the source study that produced the data, 2) the construction of the labelled task from the data, and 3) the construction of the train/test split. Appendix A details the protocol. Two questions decide a dataset’s standing as a benchmark task and organize this section. A dataset fails on task construction (Section 3.1 ) if the source study posed no real task or the archive constructed the label itself. It fails on leakage (Section 3.2 ) if the test set shares series or subjects with the training set. We further flag 65 datasets where the subjects or session identity are underspecified, so the leakage counts below are lower bounds. Whether the series index is physical time is recorded but not judged, and we return to it in Section 4 . Figure 1 summarizes the outcome of our realism provenance. 3.1 Artificial Task Construction For 52 of the 128 UCR datasets, the classification target is not a real-world prediction problem. Some labels differ from the source question or were constructed post hoc where no classification task was posed. Other source tasks were built only to exercise algorithms, with no application behind the label. While such constructed labels are best understood as pretext tasks in the sense of self-supervised learning, where pretext accuracy is a known-unreliable proxy for downstream performance [ 17 ] , UCR reports the pretext task as the benchmark result itself. We identify four mechanisms by which such labels are constructed: Metadata as label (13): the archive derives classes from a recording attribute. ItalyPowerDemand labels demand curves by season (October–March vs. April–September); ECGFiveDays labels one subject’s ECG segments by which of two recording dates they come from. Instance identity as label (14): the archive uses the recording’s source as the class, regardless of what the source study asked. In CinCECGTorso , the 2007 challenge concerned infarct location and extent [ 24 ] , but the archive labels each ECG by which of four subjects produced it; the three Pig* datasets turn a bleeding-detection study [ 13 ] into a 52-way subject-identification problem. Task replacement (13): the archive replaces the source’s label with a different task, or defines classes by its own rule where the source posed none. AllGestureWiimoteX/Y/Z were collected for user identification but are benchmarked as gesture recognition [ 14 ] ; HouseTwenty takes a smart-meter recording of one home [ 22 ] and asks whether a window is the whole-house signal or the sum of two appliances, a question the study never posed. Toy source tasks (17): the data were simulated or staged by method developers, and the classes were chosen to demonstrate a method rather than to answer any external question. ShapeletSim embeds one of two shapes in noise so that shapelet methods are guaranteed to separate them [ 2 ] ; GunPoint has two actors draw a gun or point at UCR, staged in 2003 by the archive’s curators [ 5 ] . These mechanisms are not exclusive. For example, in GunPointMaleVersusFemale , the recording was staged by the curators, and the archive then labels it by which of the two actors is performing rather than by the gun/point distinction the staging was designed around. Appendix B lists them all with their original label (if one exists) and the constructed label, and marks the overlaps. For a benchmark, the consequence is that accuracy on these tasks is a pretext score with no downstream target to validate it against: a method can rank first archive-wide by exploiting recording artifacts, subject identity or generator mechanics, none of which are the capabilities a practitioner deploying a TSC model needs. 3.2 Train/Test Leakage For 41 of the 128 UCR datasets, the test set is not independent of the training set. This happens in two ways: identical series appear in both train and test splits, or the split itself introduces leakage by grouping (or not grouping) the subjects. Additionally in 65 datasets, the information needed to check source separation is missing. To our knowledge, no systematic leakage check was run by the curators or the donors. We flag two main concerning setups: Figure 2: MiniRocket accuracy with the original training set (with duplicates, grey ) and after removing the duplicates ( blue ). On several datasets, duplication inflates test accuracy. Duplication (17 datasets): at least one test series is value-identical to a training series; in PowerCons this affects 37% of the test set ( 67 / 180 67/180 ), in Crop 16% ( 2753 / 16800 2753/16800 ), in Worms 13% ( 10 / 77 10/77 ). Same-label exact matches permit a classifier to reproduce a training label without demonstrating generalisation to a new case (see Figure 2 and Table 5 ). Shared Sources (24 datasets): whether a split is valid depends on the task. Class recognition, whose task is to predict a class for subjects unseen in training, requires the split to be grouped by subject; instance recognition, whose task is to re-identify a known subject, requires the test set to contain new recordings of that subject. On these 24 datasets one of the two rules is violated: in SemgHandMovementCh2 (class recognition) the grasps of all five subjects appear on both sides of the split; in SemgHandSubjectCh2 (instance recognition) each of the five subjects was recorded in a single session, and the repetitions of that session are split by a stratified shuffle. These pose trustworthiness challenges, as scores should state which evaluation setting they represent in benchmarking. Further details can be found in Appendix C . 4 Open Questions Do ordered sequences translate to temporal axes? The UCR archive encompasses multiple ordered datasets that span domains like spectrography and image contours. While one can argue that they provide meaningful tests for sequence models, temporal notions as warping, trends, periodicity and regime changes have no direct counterparts on a spatial or spectral axis. Treating both kinds of data as one benchmark therefore assumes a transfer the archive never tests [ 2 , 20 ] . Zhang et al. [29] provide indirect evidence: applying a single fixed permutation to every series, destroying local order while leaving each value at a fixed position, barely changes accuracy on roughly a third of the 112 equal-length UCR datasets, so those tasks are solved from aligned values rather than from order, a strategy unavailable in deployment for TSC. Should decomposed multivariate recordings count as separate datasets? Extracting one channel from a multivariate recording is a useful test of a univariate model. Counting several channels as independent datasets is a different decision: they share subjects, labels, acquisition and the underlying phenomenon [ 5 , 27 ] . Archive-wide comparisons, including rank-based tests, treat datasets as independent samples of TSC problems; derived channels violate that assumption, and one source problem receives several correlated votes in the aggregate score. How much of the problem does preprocessing solve? Every UCR series is a pre-extracted instance, and in many datasets instances are further aligned to a common reference before release, such as image outlines to a canonical starting point. The archive therefore never asks where in a stream a class-defining pattern occurs or how long it lasts. Hu et al. [15] argued that this pre-segmented setting is far removed from how classification is deployed on streams, yet the archive and the methods evaluated on it have continued to treat it as given. The consequence is that, once patterns sit at near-fixed positions, time steps become features. This offers an explanation for two recent findings: tabular classifiers are competitive on many UCR tasks [ 8 ] , and disrupting temporal order often does not meaningfully affect predictive performance [ 29 ] . Whether performance on such tasks says anything about a method’s ability to locate patterns in time, a key capability required in deployment, remains an open question. 5 Conclusion The UCR archive made univariate TSC evaluation accessible and reproducible, and they remain a reasonable instrument for comparing algorithms. Our audit, however, shows that archive-wide performance should not be interpreted uncritically as performance on real-world TSC problems. Constructed targets, train/test dependencies, preprocessing choices, non-temporal sequences and repeated source problems each break that link, and they are common enough in UCR that an aggregate ranking cannot be read as a measure of deployment readiness. We argue for evaluation that complements the archives with provenance-aware valid task selection, deployment-relevant splits and capturing the realism of deployment environments to close the gap of explored caveats. Progress requires both better scores and benchmarks that measure the intended capability. Acknowledgements Funded by the European Union. The UCR archive [ 5 ] and its multivariate counterpart, the UEA archive [ 3 ] , are the standard benchmarks for TSC. Together they comprise 158 tasks, 128 univariate and 30 multivariate, drawn from image outlines, spectroscopy and simulated processes alongside ECG, EEG, motion capture and industrial sensor recordings. Recent collections follow the same pattern at larger scale: MONSTER [ 7 ] adds substantially larger datasets, and Multiverse [ 21 ] consolidates the UEA archive, MONSTER and several domain-specific collections into 133 multivariate problems. The bake-off series [ 2 , 20 ] imposed rigor on how comparisons over these archives are run, but likewise takes the task collection as given. Prior critiques target properties of the archive’s tasks: Hu et al. [15] document the simplifications of the pre-segmented setting, Dhariyal et al. [8] show that tabular classifiers are competitive on many tasks, and Zhang et al. [29] show that temporal order is often irrelevant and the methods can emphasize on a fixed specific position rather than patterns. Each identifies a symptom without asking why the archive contains such tasks in the first place. Benchmark Construction. Recent work on AI evaluation distinguishes a benchmark as an instrument for separating algorithms from a benchmark as a proxy for downstream applicability, and warns against reading aggregate scores on convenience-driven collections as general capability [ 25 ] . Neighboring fields have responded with explicit curation: TabArena [ 10 ] admits only datasets that originate from real prediction problems and excludes derived or artificial tasks; RelBench [ 26 ] defines tasks directly on relational databases with temporally valid splits. TSC has no equivalent. Existing critiques diagnose properties of particular datasets; but we are not aware of any analysis for the origin of the tasks these datasets were collected for nor whether they represent realistic TSC applications. Our provenance analysis is a first step towards such an examination. 3 A Provenance Audit of UCR: Two Ways Its Tasks Fail as Benchmarks real task artificially constructed task (no real prediction problem) answers the source question FordA toy task staged or simulated GunPoint metadata as label a recording attribute ItalyPowerDemand instance identity as label which source produced it CinCECGTorso redefined task task swapped by the archive HouseTwenty temporal sampled over time ⋅ \cdot 71 ordered, non-temporal e.g. wavelength, contour ⋅ \cdot 49 synthetic generated ⋅ \cdot 8 38 4 11 10 8 38 2 4 5 8 …of all 128 datasets 76 12 13 14 13 no leakage found dataset contains leakage Figure 1: We show the archive datasets distribution over the different realism criterion. Our audit identifies only 38 / 128 38/128 UCR datasets as real temporal tasks; about a quarter of these are prone to split leakage. We indicate the proportion of datasets failing our leakage criteria (white boxes) and with no leakage found (black boxes) within each category, although most splits cannot be checked (53 of the 76 real-task datasets are Unclear ). We assess all 128 UCR datasets through three stages: 1) the source study that produced the data, 2) the construction of the labelled task from the data, and 3) the construction of the train/test split. Appendix A details the protocol. Two questions decide a dataset’s standing as a benchmark task and organize this section. A dataset fails on task construction (Section 3.1 ) if the source study posed no real task or the archive constructed the label itself. It fails on leakage (Section 3.2 ) if the test set shares series or subjects with the training set. We further flag 65 datasets where the subjects or session identity are underspecified, so the leakage counts below are lower bounds. Whether the series index is physical time is recorded but not judged, and we return to it in Section 4 . Figure 1 summarizes the outcome of our realism provenance. 3.1 Artificial Task Construction For 52 of the 128 UCR datasets, the classification target is not a real-world prediction problem. Some labels differ from the source question or were constructed post hoc where no classification task was posed. Other source tasks were built only to exercise algorithms, with no application behind the label. While such constructed labels are best understood as pretext tasks in the sense of self-supervised learning, where pretext accuracy is a known-unreliable proxy for downstream performance [ 17 ] , UCR reports the pretext task as the benchmark result itself. We identify four mechanisms by which such labels are constructed: Metadata as label (13): the archive derives classes from a recording attribute. ItalyPowerDemand labels demand curves by season (October–March vs. April–September); ECGFiveDays labels one subject’s ECG segments by which of two recording dates they come from. Instance identity as label (14): the archive uses the recording’s source as the class, regardless of what the source study asked. In CinCECGTorso , the 2007 challenge concerned infarct location and extent [ 24 ] , but the archive labels each ECG by which of four subjects produced it; the three Pig* datasets turn a bleeding-detection study [ 13 ] into a 52-way subject-identification problem. Task replacement (13): the archive replaces the source’s label with a different task, or defines classes by its own rule where the source posed none. AllGestureWiimoteX/Y/Z were collected for user identification but are benchmarked as gesture recognition [ 14 ] ; HouseTwenty takes a smart-meter recording of one home [ 22 ] and asks whether a window is the whole-house signal or the sum of two appliances, a question the study never posed. Toy source tasks (17): the data were simulated or staged by method developers, and the classes were chosen to demonstrate a method rather than to answer any external question. ShapeletSim embeds one of two shapes in noise so that shapelet methods are guaranteed to separate them [ 2 ] ; GunPoint has two actors draw a gun or point at UCR, staged in 2003 by the archive’s curators [ 5 ] . These mechanisms are not exclusive. For example, in GunPointMaleVersusFemale , the recording was staged by the curators, and the archive then labels it by which of the two actors is performing rather than by the gun/point distinction the staging was designed around. Appendix B lists them all with their original label (if one exists) and the constructed label, and marks the overlaps. For a benchmark, the consequence is that accuracy on these tasks is a pretext score with no downstream target to validate it against: a method can rank first archive-wide by exploiting recording artifacts, subject identity or generator mechanics, none of which are the capabilities a practitioner deploying a TSC model needs. 3.2 Train/Test Leakage For 41 of the 128 UCR datasets, the test set is not independent of the training set. This happens in two ways: identical series appear in both train and test splits, or the split itself introduces leakage by grouping (or not grouping) the subjects. Additionally in 65 datasets, the information needed to check source separation is missing. To our knowledge, no systematic leakage check was run by the curators or the donors. We flag two main concerning setups: Figure 2: MiniRocket accuracy with the original training set (with duplicates, grey ) and after removing the duplicates ( blue ). On several datasets, duplication inflates test accuracy. Duplication (17 datasets): at least one test series is value-identical to a training series; in PowerCons this affects 37% of the test set ( 67 / 180 67/180 ), in Crop 16% ( 2753 / 16800 2753/16800 ), in Worms 13% ( 10 / 77 10/77 ). Same-label exact matches permit a classifier to reproduce a training label without demonstrating generalisation to a new case (see Figure 2 and Table 5 ). Shared Sources (24 datasets): whether a split is valid depends on the task. Class recognition, whose task is to predict a class for subjects unseen in training, requires the split to be grouped by subject; instance recognition, whose task is to re-identify a known subject, requires the test set to contain new recordings of that subject. On these 24 datasets one of the two rules is violated: in SemgHandMovementCh2 (class recognition) the grasps of all five subjects appear on both sides of the split; in SemgHandSubjectCh2 (instance recognition) each of the five subjects was recorded in a single session, and the repetitions of that session are split by a stratified shuffle. These pose trustworthiness challenges, as scores should state which evaluation setting they represent in benchmarking. Further details can be found in Appendix C . 4 Open Questions Do ordered sequences translate to temporal axes? The UCR archive encompasses multiple ordered datasets that span domains like spectrography and image contours. While one can argue that they provide meaningful tests for sequence models, temporal notions as warping, trends, periodicity and regime changes have no direct counterparts on a spatial or spectral axis. Treating both kinds of data as one benchmark therefore assumes a transfer the archive never tests [ 2 , 20 ] . Zhang et al. [29] provide indirect evidence: applying a single fixed permutation to every series, destroying local order while leaving each value at a fixed position, barely changes accuracy on roughly a third of the 112 equal-length UCR datasets, so those tasks are solved from aligned values rather than from order, a strategy unavailable in deployment for TSC. Should decomposed multivariate recordings count as separate datasets? Extracting one channel from a multivariate recording is a useful test of a univariate model. Counting several channels as independent datasets is a different decision: they share subjects, labels, acquisition and the underlying phenomenon [ 5 , 27 ] . Archive-wide comparisons, including rank-based tests, treat datasets as independent samples of TSC problems; derived channels violate that assumption, and one source problem receives several correlated votes in the aggregate score. How much of the problem does preprocessing solve? Every UCR series is a pre-extracted instance, and in many datasets instances are further aligned to a common reference before release, such as image outlines to a canonical starting point. The archive therefore never asks where in a stream a class-defining pattern occurs or how long it lasts. Hu et al. [15] argued that this pre-segmented setting is far removed from how classification is deployed on streams, yet the archive and the methods evaluated on it have continued to treat it as given. The consequence is that, once patterns sit at near-fixed positions, time steps become features. This offers an explanation for two recent findings: tabular classifiers are competitive on many UCR tasks [ 8 ] , and disrupting temporal order often does not meaningfully affect predictive performance [ 29 ] . Whether performance on such tasks says anything about a method’s ability to locate patterns in time, a key capability required in deployment, remains an open question. 5 Conclusion The UCR archive made univariate TSC evaluation accessible and reproducible, and they remain a reasonable instrument for comparing algorithms. Our audit, however, shows that archive-wide performance should not be interpreted uncritically as performance on real-world TSC problems. Constructed targets, train/test dependencies, preprocessing choices, non-temporal sequences and repeated source problems each break that link, and they are common enough in UCR that an aggregate ranking cannot be read as a measure of deployment readiness. We argue for evaluation that complements the archives with provenance-aware valid task selection, deployment-relevant splits and capturing the realism of deployment environments to close the gap of explored caveats. Progress requires both better scores and benchmarks that measure the intended capability. Acknowledgements Funded by the European Union. items.summary: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.09872 (cs) [Submitted on 6 Nov 2026] Title: On the Reliability of Majority-Vote Pseudo-Labels in Test-Time Reinforcement Learning Authors: Haoyu Wang , Ru Wang , Yuanyuan Wang , Jiaxian Guo , Mingming Gong View a PDF of the paper titled On the Reliability of Majority-Vote Pseudo-Labels in Test-Time Reinforcement Learning, by Haoyu Wang and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts pretrained language models to unlabeled target-domain data using self-generated pseudo-labels, whose reliability remains poorly understood. We analyze majority-vote supervision for TTRL with online Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and decompose its error into population-majority bias and prompt-dependent finite-rollout variation. Because population-majority bias is generally unidentifiable without external supervision, we focus on mitigating the downstream effects of finite-rollout variation.
items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.09872 (cs) [Submitted on 6 Nov 2026] Title: On the Reliability of Majority-Vote Pseudo-Labels in Test-Time Reinforcement Learning Authors: Haoyu Wang , Ru Wang , Yuanyuan Wang , Jiaxian Guo , Mingming Gong View a PDF of the paper titled On the Reliability of Majority-Vote Pseudo-Labels in Test-Time Reinforcement Learning, by Haoyu Wang and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts pretrained language models to unlabeled target-domain data using self-generated pseudo-labels, whose reliability remains poorly understood. We analyze majority-vote supervision for TTRL with online Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and decompose its error into population-majority bias and prompt-dependent finite-rollout variation. Because population-majority bias is generally unidentifiable without external supervision, we focus on mitigating the downstream effects of finite-rollout variation. We propose \emph{Prompt-Conditional Distributionally Robust DPO ( this http URL )}, which conditions within-prompt robust reweighting on observed vote reliability to make updates from sampling-sensitive prompts more conservative. We further introduce a cache-based mechanism to reduce self-supervised forgetting during online adaptation. Across six mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks and five model backbones, this http URL matches or outperforms the strongest TTRL baseline in 24 of 30 settings. On the Reliability of Majority-Vote Pseudo-Labels in Test-Time Reinforcement Learning Haoyu Wang Ru Wang Yuanyuan Wang Jiaxian Guo Mingming Gong Abstract Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts pretrained language models to unlabeled target-domain data using self-generated pseudo-labels, whose reliability remains poorly understood. We analyze majority-vote supervision for TTRL with online Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and decompose its error into population-majority bias and prompt-dependent finite-rollout variation. Because population-majority bias is generally unidentifiable without external supervision, we focus on mitigating the downstream effects of finite-rollout variation. We propose Prompt-Conditional Distributionally Robust DPO (PC-Dr.DPO) , which conditions within-prompt robust reweighting on observed vote reliability to make updates from sampling-sensitive prompts more conservative. We further introduce a cache-based mechanism to reduce self-supervised forgetting during online adaptation. Across six mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks and five model backbones, PC-Dr.DPO matches or outperforms the strongest TTRL baseline in 24 of 30 settings. 1 Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence 2 The University of Melbourne 3 The University of Tokyo 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across reasoning, planning, and knowledge-intensive tasks through large-scale pretraining and post-training alignment ( OpenAI 2026 ; Google 2026 ; DeepSeek-AI 2026 ; Moonshot AI 2026 ; Qwen Team 2026 ) . However, conventional post-training is predominantly offline : model parameters are fixed before deployment and cannot adapt to shifts in the test-time input distribution. This limitation is especially important in new or specialized domains, where labeled adaptation data and reliable external verifiers may be unavailable. It motivates test-time learning methods that adapt LLMs using unlabeled target-domain inputs and signals generated by the model itself. Test-time reinforcement learning. Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts a model on unlabeled target-domain prompts using self-generated rewards ( Zuo et al. 2025 ) . Existing approaches construct such rewards from either certainty-based signals, including prediction entropy and self-certainty ( Prabhudesai et al. 2025 ; Zhao et al. 2025 ) , or ensemble-based signals, including majority-vote consistency and agreement across alternative views of an input ( Zuo et al. 2025 ; Zhang et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2025 ) . Although these methods can improve reasoning without ground-truth labels, their success depends critically on the reliability of the resulting self-supervision. Despite encouraging empirical results, this reliability remains incompletely understood. Prior work reports improvements even under imperfect or spurious rewards ( Shao et al. 2025 ) , whereas other studies highlight risks such as memorization and contamination ( Wu et al. 2025b ) . Recent work further documents failure and collapse patterns in TTRL ( He et al. 2026 ) . Nevertheless, the lack of a formal framework characterizing when self-generated pseudo-labels are reliable limits the principled design of test-time adaptation algorithms. In this work, we study majority-vote pseudo-labels for TTRL with online Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) ( Rafailov et al. 2024 ; Pang et al. 2024 ; Ko et al. 2024 ) . We identify two distinct sources of majority-vote error: (i) population-majority bias , which occurs when the behavior policy’s population-modal answer is incorrect, and (ii) finite-rollout variation , which occurs when the sampled majority differs from the population mode. The former cannot generally be identified or corrected without external supervision. The latter instead reflects sampling sensitivity and varies across prompts according to how decisively the behavior policy favors its modal answer over competing answers. Figure 1: Distribution of prompt-level modal-answer agreement for Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct on the 83-problem AMC benchmark. For each prompt x x , we sample m = 32 m=32 rollouts and compute the fraction producing the most frequent final answer. The broad distribution indicates substantial prompt-level heterogeneity: values near one correspond to nearly unanimous rollout groups, whereas smaller values indicate fragmented answer distributions that are more sensitive to resampling. This prompt-level heterogeneity is important for preference construction. Figure 1 shows the distribution of the observed modal-answer fraction for Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct on AMC. Although some prompts produce nearly unanimous rollout groups, others exhibit highly fragmented answer distributions. For the latter prompts, the selected pseudo-label is more sensitive to the particular rollout sample and may change under resampling. Existing noise-robust preference optimization methods typically employ either a shared dataset-level noise model or a globally normalized robust objective over preference pairs ( Mitchell 2023 ; Wu et al. 2025a ) . Consequently, they do not explicitly adapt the strength of robustness to the prompt-dependent reliability induced by finite-rollout sampling during test-time adaptation. Our approach: PC-Dr.DPO. To address this mismatch, we propose Prompt-Conditional Distributionally Robust DPO (PC-Dr.DPO) . PC-Dr.DPO performs robust reweighting separately within each prompt’s rollout group and adapts a prompt-specific robustness temperature using observed majority-vote reliability as a proxy for sampling sensitivity. For low-reliability prompts, the resulting reweighting emphasizes preference pairs already better satisfied by the current policy, yielding more conservative updates that mitigate the downstream optimization effects of finite-rollout errors. We further introduce a cache-based stabilization mechanism to reduce self-supervised forgetting during long-horizon online adaptation. Our contributions are threefold: • We develop a theoretical framework that separates population-majority bias from finite-rollout variation and characterizes how majority-vote errors propagate into the generalization risk of models trained on pseudo-preferences with a DPO-style objective. • We propose PC-Dr.DPO , which uses prompt-level vote reliability to adapt within-prompt robust reweighting and reduce the influence of sampling-sensitive pseudo-labels. We further introduce a cache-based mechanism to mitigate self-supervised forgetting. • We evaluate PC-Dr.DPO across six mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks and five model backbones, matching or outperforming the strongest TTRL baseline in 24 of 30 settings. 2 Preliminaries We briefly review the learning setting and the preference-optimization objectives that our analysis and method build upon. We keep the discussion minimal and focus on the notation used throughout the paper. On the Reliability of Majority-Vote Pseudo-Labels in Test-Time Reinforcement Learning Haoyu Wang Ru Wang Yuanyuan Wang Jiaxian Guo Mingming Gong Abstract Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts pretrained language models to unlabeled target-domain data using self-generated pseudo-labels, whose reliability remains poorly understood. We analyze majority-vote supervision for TTRL with online Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and decompose its error into population-majority bias and prompt-dependent finite-rollout variation. Because population-majority bias is generally unidentifiable without external supervision, we focus on mitigating the downstream effects of finite-rollout variation. We propose Prompt-Conditional Distributionally Robust DPO (PC-Dr.DPO) , which conditions within-prompt robust reweighting on observed vote reliability to make updates from sampling-sensitive prompts more conservative. We further introduce a cache-based mechanism to reduce self-supervised forgetting during online adaptation. Across six mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks and five model backbones, PC-Dr.DPO matches or outperforms the strongest TTRL baseline in 24 of 30 settings. 1 Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence 2 The University of Melbourne 3 The University of Tokyo 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across reasoning, planning, and knowledge-intensive tasks through large-scale pretraining and post-training alignment ( OpenAI 2026 ; Google 2026 ; DeepSeek-AI 2026 ; Moonshot AI 2026 ; Qwen Team 2026 ) . However, conventional post-training is predominantly offline : model parameters are fixed before deployment and cannot adapt to shifts in the test-time input distribution. This limitation is especially important in new or specialized domains, where labeled adaptation data and reliable external verifiers may be unavailable. It motivates test-time learning methods that adapt LLMs using unlabeled target-domain inputs and signals generated by the model itself. Test-time reinforcement learning. Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts a model on unlabeled target-domain prompts using self-generated rewards ( Zuo et al. 2025 ) . Existing approaches construct such rewards from either certainty-based signals, including prediction entropy and self-certainty ( Prabhudesai et al. 2025 ; Zhao et al. 2025 ) , or ensemble-based signals, including majority-vote consistency and agreement across alternative views of an input ( Zuo et al. 2025 ; Zhang et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2025 ) . Although these methods can improve reasoning without ground-truth labels, their success depends critically on the reliability of the resulting self-supervision. Despite encouraging empirical results, this reliability remains incompletely understood. Prior work reports improvements even under imperfect or spurious rewards ( Shao et al. 2025 ) , whereas other studies highlight risks such as memorization and contamination ( Wu et al. 2025b ) . Recent work further documents failure and collapse patterns in TTRL ( He et al. 2026 ) . Nevertheless, the lack of a formal framework characterizing when self-generated pseudo-labels are reliable limits the principled design of test-time adaptation algorithms. In this work, we study majority-vote pseudo-labels for TTRL with online Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) ( Rafailov et al. 2024 ; Pang et al. 2024 ; Ko et al. 2024 ) . We identify two distinct sources of majority-vote error: (i) population-majority bias , which occurs when the behavior policy’s population-modal answer is incorrect, and (ii) finite-rollout variation , which occurs when the sampled majority differs from the population mode. The former cannot generally be identified or corrected without external supervision. The latter instead reflects sampling sensitivity and varies across prompts according to how decisively the behavior policy favors its modal answer over competing answers. Figure 1: Distribution of prompt-level modal-answer agreement for Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct on the 83-problem AMC benchmark. For each prompt x x , we sample m = 32 m=32 rollouts and compute the fraction producing the most frequent final answer. The broad distribution indicates substantial prompt-level heterogeneity: values near one correspond to nearly unanimous rollout groups, whereas smaller values indicate fragmented answer distributions that are more sensitive to resampling. This prompt-level heterogeneity is important for preference construction. Figure 1 shows the distribution of the observed modal-answer fraction for Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct on AMC. Although some prompts produce nearly unanimous rollout groups, others exhibit highly fragmented answer distributions. For the latter prompts, the selected pseudo-label is more sensitive to the particular rollout sample and may change under resampling. Existing noise-robust preference optimization methods typically employ either a shared dataset-level noise model or a globally normalized robust objective over preference pairs ( Mitchell 2023 ; Wu et al. 2025a ) . Consequently, they do not explicitly adapt the strength of robustness to the prompt-dependent reliability induced by finite-rollout sampling during test-time adaptation. Our approach: PC-Dr.DPO. To address this mismatch, we propose Prompt-Conditional Distributionally Robust DPO (PC-Dr.DPO) . PC-Dr.DPO performs robust reweighting separately within each prompt’s rollout group and adapts a prompt-specific robustness temperature using observed majority-vote reliability as a proxy for sampling sensitivity. For low-reliability prompts, the resulting reweighting emphasizes preference pairs already better satisfied by the current policy, yielding more conservative updates that mitigate the downstream optimization effects of finite-rollout errors. We further introduce a cache-based stabilization mechanism to reduce self-supervised forgetting during long-horizon online adaptation. Our contributions are threefold: • We develop a theoretical framework that separates population-majority bias from finite-rollout variation and characterizes how majority-vote errors propagate into the generalization risk of models trained on pseudo-preferences with a DPO-style objective. • We propose PC-Dr.DPO , which uses prompt-level vote reliability to adapt within-prompt robust reweighting and reduce the influence of sampling-sensitive pseudo-labels. We further introduce a cache-based mechanism to mitigate self-supervised forgetting. • We evaluate PC-Dr.DPO across six mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks and five model backbones, matching or outperforming the strongest TTRL baseline in 24 of 30 settings. 2 Preliminaries We briefly review the learning setting and the preference-optimization objectives that our analysis and method build upon. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.09863 (cs) [Submitted on 6 Nov 2026] Title: Flow-Guided Target-Space Alignment via Path Consistency Authors: Ruizhi Yuan , Zeqiu Yu , Wei Gao , Wei Chen , Xiwei Tang , Lu Tang View a PDF of the paper titled Flow-Guided Target-Space Alignment via Path Consistency, by Ruizhi Yuan and 5 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Many multimodal alignment problems require mapping a source modality into a fixed space defined by a target modality, where the target space is not merely an intermediate embedding but is used directly for downstream analysis. In this setting, successful alignment should preserve both the global structure of the target distribution and the instance-level correspondence observed in paired source--target training data. Existing objectives typically address only part of this goal: contrastive losses encourage relative similarity, distribution-matching losses improve marginal agreement, and pointwise regression fits each source sample to its paired target without explicitly modeling target-space path geometry. We propose FlowAlign, a flow-guided target-space alignment method that repurposes conditional flow matching as a training-time alignment signal rather than an inference-time transport model. FlowAlign uses the learned flow field to guide the alignment of source-side representations with the fixed target space, encouraging them to preserve paired correspondence while remaining compatible with the global target-space structure. We further provide theoretical analysis showing how FlowAlign helps improve paired correspondence by controlling endpoint accuracy and capturing local target-space geometry. Experiments on synthetic data, paired single-cell multiome benchmarks, and image--text alignment demonstrate that FlowAlign improves instance level correspondence while preserving target-space structure across different modality settings. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.09846 (cs) [Submitted on 6 Nov 2026] Title: Ensemble Methodology for Reference-Free Confidence Estimation in LLM-based Code Summarization Authors: Marco Colombo , Balaji A Jayaram , Sowmyakumari Selvaraj , Sumit Tokkar , Animesh Kumar , Aravinda Prasad Sistla , Ravishankar Shetty , Rigel Gjomemo View a PDF of the paper titled Ensemble Methodology for Reference-Free Confidence Estimation in LLM-based Code Summarization, by Marco Colombo and 7 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: This paper describes an approach and use case to estimate the correctness of LLM-generated COBOL summaries without access to human-authored references. The core intuition is that inter-model agreement on semantics is informative about truth, and that an LLM-as-judge can provide higher-fidelity pairwise assessments than traditional string- or embedding-based metrics. We operationalise this intuition with (i) controlled summary generation from diverse models; (ii) a LLM evaluator that compares pairs of summaries and emits structured judgments; and (iii) a calibrated aggregation rule that combines supportive evidence while penalising only corroborated contradictions. This paper describes an approach and use case to estimate the correctness of LLM-generated COBOL summaries without access to human-authored references. The core intuition is that inter-model agreement on semantics is informative about truth, and that an LLM-as-judge can provide higher-fidelity pairwise assessments than traditional string- or embedding-based metrics ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Robinson and Kummerfeld, 2025 ) . We operationalise this intuition with (i) controlled summary generation from diverse models; (ii) a LLM evaluator that compares pairs of summaries and emits structured judgments; and (iii) a calibrated aggregation rule that combines supportive evidence while penalising only corroborated contradictions. 1. Introduction COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language) remains deeply entrenched in enterprise computing, with billions of lines of code in production across financial services, insurance, government, and healthcare sectors ( Britton, 2024 ) . These legacy systems, developed over several decades, manage mission-critical operations including transaction processing platforms (IBM TPF), core banking systems, claims processing, and regulatory compliance frameworks. The technical complexity of these codebases stems from decades of incremental modifications, vendor-specific extensions, and business logic that evolved without adequate documentation, creating significant knowledge management challenges for organizations maintaining these systems. The imperative for COBOL modernization stems from multiple converging factors. First, the steep decline in COBOL-proficient developers—with a significant portion of existing practitioners approaching retirement age and limited new talent entering the field—creates a critical sustainability risk. Second, integration challenges between legacy COBOL platforms and modern cloud-native architectures, microservices, and API ecosystems impede digital transformation initiatives. Third, maintaining aging mainframe infrastructure incurs substantial costs. These factors have given rise to multiple initiatives aimed to transform COBOL codebases into modern languages and platforms ( Gandhi et al., 2024 ; Chakravarthy et al., 2026 ) . Some of these initiatives include direct translation of COBOL codebases into a modern language ( Chakaravarthy et al., 2026 ; Froimovich et al., 2025 ; Challa et al., 2025 ) while others are focused on extracting specifications and the business logic, which can then be used to recreate that business logic in a modern language and architecture ( Bhattacharyya et al., 2025 ; Kalohia, 2026 ) . In this paper, we are focused on the latter approach, business logic extraction from COBOL codebases. The main challenge in this approach is that the vast majority of legacy COBOL programs lack adequate inline comments, external documentation, or design specifications—original developers have often retired, taking institutional knowledge with them. This creates a fundamental documentation gap: to safely migrate, refactor, or rewrite these systems, engineers need accurate descriptions of what each program does, yet manual documentation at scale is prohibitively expensive given the extensive codebases requiring analysis. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities in code understanding and documentation generation. Multiple frontier models, including GPT-4, Claude, LLaMA, and specialized code models, can generate human-readable summaries of code functionality. This creates an opportunity to automatically document legacy COBOL codebases at scale. However, a fundamental question remains: How do we evaluate the quality, accuracy, and reliability of AI-generated documentation when no ground truth exists? Traditional code summarization research relies on reference-based metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore) that measure similarity against human-authored reference summaries. These metrics are inapplicable to legacy COBOL scenarios where no reference documentation exists. LLM-based approaches. Existing approaches to assessing LLM output quality offer partial solutions but are insufficient in isolation. Reference-based metrics (BLEU ( Papineni et al., 2002 ) ), ROUGE ( ( Lin, 2004 ) ), CodeBLEU ( ( Ren et al., 2020 ) ), BERTScore ( ( Zhang et al., 2019 ) ) require human-authored ground truth summaries—fundamentally inapplicable when no reference documentation exists. Model-internal confidence signals such as perplexity and logit probabilities provide valuable indicators of generation uncertainty and can flag when models are uncertain about their predictions. However, these token-level signals cannot reliably detect when a model is confidently wrong about semantic interpretation—a model may generate a fluent, high-probability summary that completely misinterprets business logic. Single-model LLM-as-judge approaches where one model evaluates another’s output show promise but face validity concerns: evaluators may have systematic biases or blind spots, lack deep understanding of COBOL-specific constructs and mainframe paradigms, have no ground truth for calibration, and can themselves produce inconsistent assessments. No single metric adequately addresses the multifaceted challenge of reference-free evaluation for domain-specific legacy code. Challenge: No human-authored references. In the absence of human-authored references, how can we quantitatively estimate confidence in LLM-generated COBOL documentation to determine which outputs are reliable enough for operational use and which require human expert review? This requires evaluation metrics that are: reference-free (operable without ground truth comparisons); quantifiable (producing numerical confidence scores supporting prioritization and quality gating); interpretable (providing actionable signals explaining why outputs are flagged as low-confidence); multi-dimensional (assessing correctness, completeness, and consistency across multiple quality axes); robust (resistant to single-model biases and prompt engineering artifacts); and scalable (applicable to millions of lines of code requiring documentation). For enterprise adoption, organizations need confidence metrics that indicate: “This summary has high inter-model agreement and complete code coverage—safe for downstream use” versus “This summary has contradictions and potential omissions—requires expert review.” Our approach: overview. We propose a multi-metric ensemble framework that combines complementary evaluation mechanisms: (1) Inter-model agreement via LLM-as-judge: generating summaries from multiple diverse models and employing structured pairwise comparisons; (2) Calibrated aggregation: combining judgments through linear pooling with conjunctive penalty for corroborated contradictions; (3) Token-level confidence scores: measuring generation certainty through perplexity and logit probability analysis; (4) Code coverage assessment: employing G-Eval metrics to quantify documentation completeness. This reference-free framework enables automatic triage of AI-generated documentation. Our approach has been implemented inside Infosys to deal with summarization of large code bases and extraction of business rules from those code bases for developers. This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 contains backgroun and related work. Section 3 describes our approach in detail. Section 4 describes the evaluation of our approach and results, and Section 5 concludes the paper. 2. Background and Related Work CODE-NN ( Iyer et al., 2016 ) introduced the first fully data-driven, end-to-end neural approach to code summarization, using LSTM networks with an attention mechanism to generate natural language descriptions of C# code snippets and SQL queries. The model was trained on a corpus automatically mined from StackOverflow, sidestepping the need for hand-labeled data. Building on this attentional encoder-decoder paradigm, code2vec ( Alon et al., 2019 ) took a different angle, representing code as a fixed-length vector by decomposing it into paths through its abstract syntax tree (AST) and learning to aggregate those paths; trained on roughly 14 million methods, it was shown to predict method names accurately even on previously unseen code and to capture meaningful semantic relationships between code snippets. Code2seq ( Alon et al., 2018 ) extended this AST-path idea into a full sequence-generation setting, using attention over the same compositional AST paths to decode natural language sequences rather than single labels, and it outperformed prior token-sequence-based neural machine translation models across multiple languages and tasks, including code summarization and code captioning. DeepCom ( Hu et al., 2018 ) approached the problem as a structure-aware machine translation task, applying NLP techniques together with structural information extracted from Java methods to automatically generate descriptive comments, and it demonstrated clear gains in BLEU-4 scores over earlier baselines like CODE-NN by better capturing the semantics of source code rather than just its token sequence. Finally, the Transformer-based approach of Ahmad et al. ( Ahmad et al., 2020 ) replaced recurrent architectures with a self-attention Transformer model for encoding code, finding that relative position encoding of code tokens (rather than the absolute encoding used in standard Transformers) substantially improved performance; combined with copy attention, this simple adaptation outperformed prior state-of-the-art techniques by a significant margin and has since become a common baseline architecture in the field. Together, these five papers trace the field’s progression from RNN/LSTM-based sequence models, through AST-path-based structural representations, to Transformer architectures explicitly adapted to the syntactic properties of code. Code summarization models are commonly evaluated using a combination of lexical overlap, syntactic awareness, and semantic similarity metrics. BLEU ( Papineni et al., 2002 ) measures the n-gram overlap between a generated summary and one or more reference summaries, emphasizing precision by rewarding exact word sequence matches. ROUGE ( Lin, 2004 ) focuses on recall and evaluates how much of the reference summary is captured by the generated text, with variants such as ROUGE-N and ROUGE-L measuring n-gram and longest common subsequence overlap, respectively. To better assess code-related text generation, CodeBLEU ( Ren et al., 2020 ) extends BLEU by incorporating programming-language-specific features, including weighted n-gram matching, abstract syntax tree (AST) similarity, and data-flow consistency, providing a more comprehensive evaluation of code understanding and generation quality. In contrast, BERTScore ( Zhang et al., 2019 ) leverages contextual embeddings from pre-trained transformer models to measure semantic similarity between generated and reference summaries, allowing it to capture meaning even when different words or phrasing are used. Together, these metrics provide complementary perspectives on code summarization quality, ranging from surface-level lexical agreement to deeper semantic and structural correctness. 3. The first step of the approach includes parsing and static analysis of the COBOL code to understand dependencies among paragraphs, build a call graph, and extract other types of information. Pairwise comparisons with an LLM-as-judge yield structured scores, which are then aggregated into a final confidence estimate. 3.1. Pairwise Evaluation via LLM-as-Judge Traditional reference-based metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore) correlate imperfectly with human judgments for code summarisation and are sensitive to surface form and identifier overlap—a poor fit for reference-free settings. Prompted LLM judges, by contrast, have shown strong correlation with human ratings on code tasks ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Robinson and Kummerfeld, 2025 ) . We therefore instantiate a dedicated OpenAI model 𝒥 \mathcal{J} as an evaluator that compares pairs of summaries following a list of criteria L = { L 1 , … , L n } L=\{L_{1},...,L_{n}\} specifying the task to the LLM and the outputs (See Appendix for the list used in the evaluation). Anchored, pairwise comparisons. We conduct two comparisons anchored on the Infosys output: E 1 = 𝒥 ⁡ ( S 1 , S 0 ) , E 2 = 𝒥 ⁡ ( S 2 , S 0 ) . E_{1}=\mathcal{J}(S_{1},S_{0}),\qquad E_{2}=\mathcal{J}(S_{2},S_{0}). Each evaluation returns a structured JSON record E i = ( agreement i , score i , missing_details i , contradictions i , rationale i ) . E_{i}=(\texttt{agreement}_{i},\ \texttt{score}_{i},\ \texttt{missing\_details}_{i},\ \texttt{contradictions}_{i},\\ \texttt{rationale}_{i}). The agreement label is one of Agree / Mostly Agree / Disagree ; the score is a continuous confidence on [ 0 , 10 ] [0,10] tied to a list of criteria that emphasises functional equivalence (purpose, logic, inputs, outputs) and discounts mere wording differences. The missing-details and contradictions fields enumerate omissions and logical conflicts, respectively, and the rationale gives a concise justification. These fields serve both downstream explainability and manual auditability. Granularity control. A common failure mode in pairwise judging is spurious disagreement caused by mismatched levels of detail . To mitigate this, all generators use prompts that mirror Infosys’ template, and evaluators are instructed to: (i) ignore stylistic paraphrase; (ii) treat minor omissions as Mostly Agree if they do not alter semantics; and (iii) reserve Disagree for contradictions or omissions that change behaviour. This alignment makes disagreements diagnostic rather than an artefact of verbosity mismatches. 3.2. Token-Level Confidence via Perplexity While inter-model agreement provides evidence of semantic consistency, it does not capture the generation certainty of individual summaries. A model may produce a fluent output that agrees with others yet internally exhibit high uncertainty during generation. To address this, we incorporate token-level confidence scores derived from the model’s output probability distribution. Logit probabilities and perplexity. Modern LLM APIs support returning log-probabilities for generated tokens when the logprobs parameter is enabled. For each token t i t_{i} in a generated summary S = { t 1 , t 2 , … , t n } S=\{t_{1},t_{2},\dots,t_{n}\} , the model provides log ⁡ P ⁡ ( t i ∣ t < i , C ) \log P(t_{i}\mid t_{<i},C) , representing the log-probability of token t i t_{i} given the preceding context and COBOL input C C . We compute the perplexity of a generated summary as (1) PPL ( S ) = exp ( − 1 n ∑ i = 1 n log P ( t i ∣ t < i , C ) ) . \mathrm{PPL}(S)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log P(t_{i}\mid t_{<i},C)\right). Perplexity measures how “surprised” the model is by its own generation: lower perplexity indicates higher confidence, while higher perplexity suggests the model struggled to predict subsequent tokens. For enterprise applications, perplexity provides a reference-free signal identifying generations where the model exhibited uncertainty—even if the output appears superficially fluent. Approach A high level view of our approach is depicted in Figure 1 . The first step of the approach includes parsing and static analysis of the COBOL code to understand dependencies among paragraphs, build a call graph, and extract other types of information. The output of this step is a set of code chunks, each of which is summarized as a unit in the next steps. Determining the correct granularity of this step is an important aspect of our approach. At one end, chunks at the level of single instructions create verbose descriptions that are not useful. At another extreme, chunks that include whole programs create summaries that hide important details and are not useful. After experimenting with different granularities, we settle for chunks at the paragraph and function level. Let C C denote a COBOL code chunk dedicated to a single functionality. Importantly, the chunking policy is not under our control: the segmentation into summarisation units is predetermined by the Infosys pipeline. Our method therefore treats the Infosys chunking as fixed and operates downstream. This constraint reflects realistic deployment conditions, where third-party enterprise tooling governs preprocessing. We assume a set of auxiliary descriptions for called paragraphs or programs, 𝒟 = { ( n i , d i ) } i = 1 m \mathcal{D}=\{(n_{i},d_{i})\}_{i=1}^{m} , where n i n_{i} is a callee name and d i d_{i} is a fixed, vetted English description. These include descriptions of called paragraphs/functions. These dependency descriptions are injected into prompts and not reconstructed per run, both to reduce variance and to keep the evaluation focused on the behaviour of C C . In addition, the prompt is also augmented with a list of criteria L = { L 1 , … , L n } L=\{L_{1},...,L_{n}\} specifying the task to the LLM and the outputs (See Appendix for the list used in the evaluation). Specifically, the list L L contains the criteria decided by Infosys in their prompt. We consider three summarisation systems: M 0 = Infosys (OpenAI-based) , M 1 = LLaMA 3.3-70B , M 2 = Grok-3 . M_{0}=\text{Infosys (OpenAI-based)},\ M_{1}=\text{LLaMA\,3.3-70B},\ M_{2}=\text{Grok-3}. S_{0}\leftarrow M_{0}(C,\mathcal{D}),\ S_{1}\leftarrow M_{1}(C,\mathcal{D}),\ S_{2}\leftarrow M_{2}(C,\mathcal{D}). Model diversity is desirable but the method is agnostic to the specific choices so long as the models are competent summarizers and not identically trained; the ensemble logic extends to k > 3 k>3 models. Pairwise comparisons with an LLM-as-judge yield structured scores, which are then aggregated into a final confidence estimate. 3.1. Pairwise Evaluation via LLM-as-Judge Traditional reference-based metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore) correlate imperfectly with human judgments for code summarisation and are sensitive to surface form and identifier overlap—a poor fit for reference-free settings. Prompted LLM judges, by contrast, have shown strong correlation with human ratings on code tasks ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Robinson and Kummerfeld, 2025 ) . We therefore instantiate a dedicated OpenAI model 𝒥 \mathcal{J} as an evaluator that compares pairs of summaries following a list of criteria L = { L 1 , … , L n } L=\{L_{1},...,L_{n}\} specifying the task to the LLM and the outputs (See Appendix for the list used in the evaluation). Anchored, pairwise comparisons. We conduct two comparisons anchored on the Infosys output: E 1 = 𝒥 ⁡ ( S 1 , S 0 ) , E 2 = 𝒥 ⁡ ( S 2 , S 0 ) . E_{1}=\mathcal{J}(S_{1},S_{0}),\qquad E_{2}=\mathcal{J}(S_{2},S_{0}). Each evaluation returns a structured JSON record E i = ( agreement i , score i , missing_details i , contradictions i , rationale i ) . E_{i}=(\texttt{agreement}_{i},\ \texttt{score}_{i},\ \texttt{missing\_details}_{i},\ \texttt{contradictions}_{i},\\ \texttt{rationale}_{i}). The agreement label is one of Agree / Mostly Agree / Disagree ; the score is a continuous confidence on [ 0 , 10 ] [0,10] tied to a list of criteria that emphasises functional equivalence (purpose, logic, inputs, outputs) and discounts mere wording differences. The missing-details and contradictions fields enumerate omissions and logical conflicts, respectively, and the rationale gives a concise justification. These fields serve both downstream explainability and manual auditability. Granularity control. A common failure mode in pairwise judging is spurious disagreement caused by mismatched levels of detail . To mitigate this, all generators use prompts that mirror Infosys’ template, and evaluators are instructed to: (i) ignore stylistic paraphrase; (ii) treat minor omissions as Mostly Agree if they do not alter semantics; and (iii) reserve Disagree for contradictions or omissions that change behaviour. This alignment makes disagreements diagnostic rather than an artefact of verbosity mismatches. 3.2. This is the equal-weight linear pool, preserving interpretability (two 10s average to 10) and reflecting the standard practice of combining expert scores via averaging. Financial paper that is insured by the FDIC's Temporary Liquidity Guarantee Program is not excluded from relevant indexes, nor is any financial or nonfinancial commercial paper that may be directly or indirectly affected by one or more of the Federal Reserve's liquidity facilities. This rate replaces that for adjustment credit, which was discontinued after January 8, 2003. For further information, see www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/press/bcreg/2002/200210312/default.htm . The rate reported is that for the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Historical series for the rate on adjustment credit as well as the rate on primary credit are available at www.federalreserve.gov/releases/h15/data.htm . 9. The 30-year Treasury constant maturity series was discontinued on February 18, 2002, and reintroduced on February 9, 2006. From February 18, 2002, to February 9, 2006, the U.S. Treasury published a factor for adjusting the daily nominal 20-year constant maturity in order to estimate a 30-year nominal rate. The historical adjustment factor can be found at home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics . Source: U.S. Treasury. 10. Yields on Treasury inflation protected securities (TIPS) adjusted to constant maturities. Source: U.S. Treasury. Additional information on both nominal and inflation-indexed yields may be found at home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics . 11. Based on the unweighted average bid yields for all TIPS with remaining terms to maturity of more than 10 years. Note: Current and historical H.15 data, along with weekly, monthly, and annual averages, are available on the Board's Data Download Program (DDP) at www.federalreserve.gov/datadownload/Choose.aspx?rel=H15 ). Weekly, monthly and annual rates are averages of business days unless otherwise noted. Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: November 09, 2026 Back to Top

items.content:
An encoder (optical system) maps objects to noiseless images, which noise corrupts into measurements. Our information estimator uses only these noisy measurements and a noise model to quantify how well measurements distinguish objects.

Many imaging systems produce measurements that humans never see or cannot interpret directly. Your smartphone processes raw sensor data through algorithms before producing the final photo. MRI scanners collect frequency-space measurements that require reconstruction before doctors can view them. Self-driving cars process camera and LiDAR data directly with neural networks.

What matters in these systems is not how measurements look, but how much useful information they contain. AI can extract this information even when it is encoded in ways that humans cannot interpret.

And yet we rarely evaluate information content directly. Traditional metrics like resolution and signal-to-noise ratio assess individual aspects of quality separately, making it difficult to compare systems that trade off between these factors. The common alternative, training neural networks to reconstruct or classify images, conflates the quality of the imaging hardware with the quality of the algorithm.

We developed a framework that enables direct evaluation and optimization of imaging systems based on their information content. In our NeurIPS 2025 paper, we show that this information metric predicts system performance across four imaging domains, and that optimizing it produces designs that match state-of-the-art end-to-end methods while requiring less memory, less compute, and no task-specific decoder design.

Why mutual information?

Mutual information quantifies how much a measurement reduces uncertainty about the object that produced it. Two systems with the same mutual information are equivalent in their ability to distinguish objects, even if their measurements look completely different.

This single number captures the combined effect of resolution, noise, sampling, and all other factors that affect measurement quality. A blurry, noisy image that preserves the features needed to distinguish objects can contain more information than a sharp, clean image that loses those features.


Information unifies traditionally separate quality metrics. It accounts for noise, resolution, and spectral sensitivity together rather than treating them as independent factors.

Previous attempts to apply information theory to imaging faced two problems. The first approach treated imaging systems as unconstrained communication channels, ignoring the physical limitations of lenses and sensors. This produced wildly inaccurate estimates. The second approach required explicit models of the objects being imaged, limiting generality.

Our method avoids both problems by estimating information directly from measurements.

Estimating information from measurements

Estimating mutual information between high-dimensional variables is notoriously difficult. Sample requirements grow exponentially with dimensionality, and estimates suffer from high bias and variance.

However, imaging systems have properties that enable decomposing this hard problem into simpler subproblems. Mutual information can be written as:

\[I(X; Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)\]

The first term, $H(Y)$, measures total variation in measurements from both object differences and noise. The second term, $H(Y \mid X)$, measures variation from noise alone.


Mutual information equals the difference between total measurement variation and noise-only variation.

Imaging systems have well-characterized noise. Photon shot noise follows a Poisson distribution. Electronic readout noise is Gaussian. This known noise physics means we can compute $H(Y \mid X)$ directly, leaving only $H(Y)$ to be learned from data.

For $H(Y)$, we fit a probabilistic model (e.g. a transformer or other autoregressive model) to a dataset of measurements. The model learns the distribution of all possible measurements. We tested three models spanning efficiency-accuracy tradeoffs: a stationary Gaussian process (fastest), a full Gaussian (intermediate), and an autoregressive PixelCNN (most accurate). The approach provides an upper bound on true information; any modeling error can only overestimate, never underestimate.

Validation across four imaging domains

Information estimates should predict decoder performance if they capture what limits real systems. We tested this relationship across four imaging applications.


Information estimates predict decoder performance across color photography, radio astronomy, lensless imaging, and microscopy. Higher information consistently produces better results on downstream tasks.

Color photography. Digital cameras encode color using filter arrays that restrict each pixel to detect only certain wavelengths. We compared three filter designs: the traditional Bayer pattern, a random arrangement, and a learned arrangement. Information estimates correctly ranked which designs would produce better color reconstructions, matching the rankings from neural network demosaicing without requiring any reconstruction algorithm.

Radio astronomy. Telescope arrays achieve high angular resolution by combining signals from sites across the globe. Selecting optimal telescope locations is computationally intractable because each site’s value depends on all others. Information estimates predicted reconstruction quality across telescope configurations, enabling site selection without expensive image reconstruction.

Lensless imaging. Lensless cameras replace traditional optics with light-modulating masks. Their measurements bear no visual resemblance to scenes. Information estimates predicted reconstruction accuracy across a lens, microlens array, and diffuser design at various noise levels.

Microscopy. LED array microscopes use programmable illumination to generate different contrast modes. Information estimates correlated with neural network accuracy at predicting protein expression from cell images, enabling evaluation without expensive protein labeling experiments.

In all cases, higher information meant better downstream performance.

Designing systems with IDEAL

Information estimates can do more than evaluate existing systems. Our Information-Driven Encoder Analysis Learning (IDEAL) method uses gradient ascent on information estimates to optimize imaging system parameters.


IDEAL optimizes imaging system parameters through gradient feedback on information estimates, without requiring a decoder network.

The standard approach to computational imaging design, end-to-end optimization, jointly trains the imaging hardware and a neural network decoder. This requires backpropagating through the entire decoder, creating memory constraints and potential optimization difficulties.

IDEAL avoids these problems by optimizing the encoder alone. We tested it on color filter design. Starting from a random filter arrangement, IDEAL progressively improved the design. The final result matched end-to-end optimization in both information content and reconstruction quality.


IDEAL matches end-to-end optimization performance while avoiding decoder complexity during training.

Implications

Information-based evaluation creates new possibilities for rigorous assessment of imaging systems in real-world conditions. Current approaches require either subjective visual assessment, ground truth data that is unavailable in deployment, or isolated metrics that miss overall capability. Our method provides an objective, unified metric from measurements alone.

The computational efficiency of IDEAL suggests possibilities for designing imaging systems that were previously intractable. By avoiding decoder backpropagation, the approach reduces memory requirements and training complexity. We explore these capabilities more extensively in follow-on work.

The framework may extend beyond imaging to other sensing domains. Any system that can be modeled as deterministic encoding with known noise characteristics could benefit from information-based evaluation and design, including electronic, biological, and chemical sensors.

This post is based on our NeurIPS 2025 paper “Information-driven design of imaging systems”. Code is available on GitHub. A video summary is available on the project website.

MRI scanners collect frequency-space measurements that require reconstruction before doctors can view them. Self-driving cars process camera and LiDAR data directly with neural networks.

What matters in these systems is not how measurements look, but how much useful information they contain. AI can extract this information even when it is encoded in ways that humans cannot interpret.

And yet we rarely evaluate information content directly. Traditional metrics like resolution and signal-to-noise ratio assess individual aspects of quality separately, making it difficult to compare systems that trade off between these factors.
